item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Engine, Not Aerodynamics, Was the Blocker
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/

item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and now it's being sent to power data centers first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because the sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and now it's being sent to power data centers first.

The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building engines in-house and pivoting to data center power generation, with concrete numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's answer to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet but to use the atmosphere's own refractive power to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls it boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff. The boom is still generated at the aircraft, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So you can't go full speed over land, but a 9am departure from New York and a 9:30am landing in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean nobody is listening, so full speed is fine. Push the logic to its limit and you get the line: if there is no sonic boom at all, there is nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The US ban on overland supersonic flight, in place since 1973, ended on June 6 last year. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be reversed by the next person, so he turned to pushing legislation through Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He puts the significance plainly: supersonic is not a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote count. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to statute turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, the split with Rolls-Royce was public, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch in-house — and not just design it, but manufacture the hardest parts, like turbine blades, themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at full power for long periods at Mach 1.7 temperatures, with the fan removed from the front and a generator bolted on the back, is a power generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application is not in the sky but on the ground. Take off the fan, put a generator on the back, drop it into a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake specifically calls out that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial point of this path: before the supersonic airliner has its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it is selling to the buyer that is least short of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine into ground power first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success is not guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over the ocean, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — aviation engines are normally validated by accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, with the actual price most likely higher — and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he states plainly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, cannot give a firm date, and only commits to delivering at the earliest time physically possible — which from the outside looks like around 2030. There is a tradeoff worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it is unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data center demand is so large they plan to auction it
Asked whether the data center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine fires up next month, and then they intend to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he has talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this passage is the anomalous supply-demand signal it gives: for a power product not yet in mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has gone from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake walks through how fast the regulatory push moved: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, posted it, Elon reposted, flew to Washington that night to start lobbying for legalization, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday the aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it is still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he thinks is slow but admits would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a single technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why renaming a charity is more dangerous than renaming a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff more at risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps became Prosper Global not because the strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a rename can put staff more at risk.

Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster response and the logic of the rename; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI entering aid work, is worth more.

4:21 The rename isn't a new strategy — the old name no longer fits the business
Jada says an organization's identity grows up the way a person does. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the merciful giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, using blockchain for identity management, and the response she gets is flatly: "That has nothing to do with your name." The rename isn't a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global is meant to shorten the conversation and put the values up front: we believe every person has the capacity to prosper, not just to survive.

6:31 Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize the Mercy Corps colors and know who to look for. A rename means a phased rollout, one country at a time, with local people judging the timing and the context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this is not an ordinary corporate logo swap — in the short term it may put frontline staff more at risk. The interesting part: 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the rename — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

8:37 Syria is the clearest case for the rename logic
Jada drove from Aleppo to Damascus and saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just come out of 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is flowing back in rather than out, with millions returning home at the same time. But many are still living in camps, and the communities they return to have no working water systems and destroyed houses. She tells the story of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she hadn't worked before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating land. Prosper Global helped her set up drip irrigation and repair the local water system, and along the way she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought another group of women along with her. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare pieces of good news, and it has been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar and Lebanon. The mechanism: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't work out what to plant or which inputs they can afford, some of them decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for today — it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid organizations are themselves paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global has just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine's harvest this year is actually decent, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially grain silos and storage facilities, with drones. The logic is simple: even with a good harvest, if the silos and storage are bombed out, or the roads and ports are hit so the grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries, and it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention costs about seven times less than response, and nobody wants to fund it
Jada says there's a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to fund only life-saving aid, which is in fact the least efficient way to do it. Her number: doing prevention, trying to stop a crisis before it happens, costs roughly seven times less than intervening afterward. She also says they were ready to rename to Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off because they needed to read the situation — the funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a hard place. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid actually looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

19:59 With USAID gone, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture, in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help" — it's that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you and has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the program level: accessing best practices, pinpointing more precisely what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found the magic solution yet, but they're talking to AI companies, hoping to build something together that genuinely changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks on international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is part of a broader trend. She sees the first case treated as a deliberate pattern as Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges and other civilian infrastructure that was traditionally untouchable followed quickly. Then the pattern spread to the way the war is fought in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have a hospital network, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now those rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to a lot of people.

item.title: In the AI Era the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence, It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth hearing for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is middling in information density; the pricing, audit, and sales mechanics in the back half are worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if a whole data center full of geniuses showed up tomorrow at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, those institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change the way they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years isn't getting access to intelligence, it's wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. It also explains why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches, each with different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says the companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that end state, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through that phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the end state is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give them the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow of an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst and get a revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, while automatically notifying the junior analysts on the deal and showing a full audit trail of every small change. He points out the key thing: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only come from someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork against ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are far better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there's a pile of microservices in the head — how knowledge is stored, how it's retrieved, how it's triggered, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers the memory of some event, which produces a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip seat-based pricing and go straight to outcome-based
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal signed needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human involvement, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every company goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage-based, then to outcome-based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage entirely and ask the customer directly: how much do I charge you per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two get conflated all the time. The logic: if the answer is wrong and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As the tool moves from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided the way it did, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, a decision you can't explain doesn't get past the gate.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and that content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard showing the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on; it's connected to the company's various systems and is very clear about company goals, values, what has to be delivered to customers, and the north star metric, so it shapes every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how do I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you, ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with before want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in and give it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be turned down by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: there were no star investors on the cap table yet, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And not the send-a-deck-no-interest kind — it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe,’ ‘like Gabe, talk for an hour,’ ‘come to IC,’ ‘grab a meal,’ ‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time they said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and none of them believe in me? He sums up the three reasons investors passed: they underestimated the finance TAM, the product really was bad at the time, and there weren't enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, but It Became a Landmark Philadelphia Can't Tear Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's standing is given by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, left to sit in a warehouse — and in the end what saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's standing is given by its audience, not by the experts.

Thirty minutes, one complete narrative arc: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam decided its fate
In Rocky III there's a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department make a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after filming. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: the material wasn't something you throw away after the shoot, it was fine-art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a ‘euphemism’ for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia, permanently, at the top of the steps. Precisely because it was bronze and not foam, the fifty-year fight that followed was even possible.

10:25 The opposition was rooted in Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it most fiercely, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century; by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts world wanted to remake Philadelphia as a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — ‘the Athens of the Western world.’ They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they didn't see how a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdomened boxer could help Philadelphia get there. The art commission's chairman, F. Eugene Dixon Jr., wrote to a colleague that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but putting it permanently in the courtyard — ‘I hope you're joking.’ In the winter of 1980 the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement; the remaining two votes were to ban it from the steps outright.

12:34 Thousands of signatures were no match for eight people with votes
It was a grassroots campaign that hauled the statue back from Los Angeles to Philadelphia. A local truck driver, Art Gorman, was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a straight-talking Philly guy from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed sophisticates, the taste gatekeepers, to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum. At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a ‘slobs versus snobs’ narrative. But the petition couldn't change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew had bolted the statue into the ground with steel rods
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission only allowed the statue back on the steps for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and the museum was left to deal with it. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel rods driven several feet into the ground — ‘as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever.’ In the end the statue was pried loose and trucked five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over; in fact, over the next twenty-five years Stallone repeatedly asked to bring it back to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public-space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns — who had appeared in the sequels and was a well-connected Philadelphia lawyer — called the mayor and asked whether he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum trustees invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then to hell with them. The mayor said, all right, to hell with them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise they worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — off to one side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on a local NPR call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, ‘but that's not a work of art.’ The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was an image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said that ideally he wanted the statue at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs would never let that happen, and he called Baum a snob and an insult to the audience. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 to approve, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolism had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and lifted onto a brand-new granite pedestal.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting, in which nine people were killed, set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo — known for violent policing and racist demagoguery — became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted to build, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those boxers were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze falls far short of a real champion: ‘His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran up are called the Rocky steps.’

28:21 In the reckoning over monuments, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue put up for a fictional white movie character, taking the place of a real Black champion; its time should have been up. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign on it reading ‘no justice, no peace,’ early in the pandemic it was given a face mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired, his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family posing for a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K Injection Refusal Rate Has Doubled, and Infant Brain Hemorrhage Is Preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
