item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but in the US the refusal rate has risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but in the US the refusal rate has risen from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanism of newborn hemorrhage and the discovery of vitamin K plus how the 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The back half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplements during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome and very little self-synthesized K2, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter, and a exclusively breastfed infant takes in less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often comes with no warning, straight to brain hemorrhage
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. Late is the most dangerous: about 60% of cases are intracranial hemorrhage, and there is often no warning bleed beforehand, just sudden brain hemorrhage, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by "the bleeding probability is low."

25:46 One intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K shot at birth is recommended. It provides a stable supply through the first months, cutting late bleeding risk from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but they require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, are less effective than injection, and no oral formulation is approved by regulators in the US.

44:27 How the 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was "vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants." In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows the fallout from a single overdose incident can last decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare has never fully cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral dosing and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and Britain's injection rate fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But the two studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never fully recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates have doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
In the US, refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusals fall into three categories, and the birth attendant matters enormously
Reasons for refusal fall roughly into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of "natural birth," and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some believe that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; some interpret a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as "you are not fit to be a mother." Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning to give birth at home or in a birth center. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own child; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: speaking publicly to say "I made this decision, this is the consequence, don't do what I did." At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusal and administration, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep increasing.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Drain
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting a child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting a child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single topic on a parenting podcast. But if you're dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth a listen.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak sentences, and recognize dinosaurs, but his grandmother always makes him "perform" — repeat what he's learned, clap — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often think connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But this is "fast-food connection" — the child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection goes both ways: not only do we make children perform, we ourselves are often performing rather than being ourselves. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction from babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted, and the payoff was tiny and fleeting — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection, it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches children to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches children to be insincere — everything we do with children teaches them something, and this teaches "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are charismatic to us not because of how they present themselves or what they put out, but because they are genuinely interested in us and paying attention to us. Children need this especially, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist regarded as a parenting expert, in which the author, now a grandparent, said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate judgment: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate games, wanting the child to cooperate, she was "operating" rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see, don't fake interest
The concrete approach: treat the child as a person with depth, talent, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you're lining them up." Not faking interest, but genuinely becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you let go of the fear that "this is bad for the child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents treat me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even with frequent contact, children can put it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach her mother or correct her, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he won't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that," but say to her son "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting, and it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.title: The Pentagon doesn't lack models — it lacks the chain that puts intelligence on the president's desk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-五角大楼不缺模型-缺的是把情报送到总统桌上的那条链/
item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft. It was procurement reform, an institutionalized intelligence-analysis shop, and a chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it — APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft. It was procurement reform, an institutionalized intelligence-analysis shop, and a chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it — APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out clearly where the government's AI integration bottleneck is; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose conversational interview with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle wasn't the plane, it was the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together the way they did, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the exact inverse: the technology comes from the commercial world and moves too fast, and it has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is moving fastest in warfighting, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other departments have made clear progress in warfighting spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and get intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that systems should no longer be split into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because to support the front you need data that is clean, organized and usable at the tempo of operations, and those business systems were never built for that tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and there has to be clear value in it. Worse, the systems the government gave them are already bad to use — you're making it hard to enter data while demanding a big drop in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that a company that doesn't do AI gets eliminated, but the Air Force or the national security system won't be ‘competed out’ — that kind of forcing function comes along once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our ability to manufacture mechanisms ourselves. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take weird career paths, and let people who don't move fast enough face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn money and hit the pits first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2: the technology happens in the commercial sector first and then goes into government, so government has a second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you understand token economics first and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if it gets this right it can act as a super-sized buyer and negotiate bulk pricing.

23:20 To put GPUs in the field, first clear the policy that assigns blame for a signature
Garrett says if you put these tools in soldiers' hands, you'd be shocked at how innovatively and cleverly they use them for their actual jobs — which may mean pushing compute to the edge and putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips, and who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we're taking that risk’ — and if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately opaque — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality, so you can build benchmarks from it. Still, it's only one input to a decision — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and people will bill more hours
Garrett says the government buys a great deal on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure carries a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to bill more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement when the hours run out, they'll bill more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data there's no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is far below that level.

item.title: Procrastination Is Not a Willpower Problem: You'll Fail With the Same Plan Next Time
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-clearerthink-拖延不是意志力问题-下次你还会用同一个计划失败/
item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about 20% of adults do it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: without changing the plan, the result won't change.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it's harmful, and about 20% of adults do it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need different fixes, but they share one premise: without changing the plan, the result won't change.

It breaks procrastination into types you can treat, and gives a concrete toolbox instead of another 'self-discipline' pep talk. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination hides reluctance
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we don't intend to delay it, and we know it's bad for us. So 'deliberately deciding to do it later and feeling fine about it' is not procrastination. The gray area: what if you think delaying is good for you but it's actually harmful? His test is 'could you have expected this to be better for you.' About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically, and among students it's 50%. He stresses that procrastination doesn't only happen to people who don't care; people high in conscientiousness, genuinely productive, who really want to make an impact, procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is many types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see it happening to people outside student populations, and you can't address it in practice. Because a student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout, and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes anxiety-driven, externally tempted, and burnout-driven types, plus one he calls the zigzagger — closer to ADHD and impulsivity, switching back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety has two faces: fear of the task or fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this hurts, the brain says I don't want to hurt, so you put it off. But anxiety also has an adaptive side — if what you're anxious about isn't the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety actually pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it's aimed at; and if you also feel you're incapable of finishing, anxiety more easily turns into paralysis. Itamar adds: even when anxiety drives you, it's a dangerous source of motivation, because it brings stress and a worse experience along with it.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you'll try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and use more willpower, you'll do it. The absurdity is that we see it fail again and again, yet believe it again and again. Reasons include the bias blind spot (failing to recognize your own biases) and the empathy gap (predicting, in a calm state, what you'll do when you're in a hot emotional state). The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: if nothing changes, the result won't change.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach: don't assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower; instead ask 'for someone a lot like me, what would help them get this done in two weeks' — set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination is not a time management problem, even excellent time management can fail, what you should do is distance management. Calling yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of 'I', or asking 'what advice would I give a friend', all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, see through the situation and bypass biases.

16:13 Anxiety type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For anxiety-driven procrastinators, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing is overestimating the probability that something bad will happen and also overestimating how much it will hurt you. For example, 'there's a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and tell everyone to blacklist me too.' The method is to ask: how likely is this to happen? If it did happen, how big would the impact be? If it happened, how could I move on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit in that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway, which he calls metacognitive awareness. Itamar places it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it self-reinforces
Spencer points out that anxiety creates anxiety: once you say 'I won't do it now,' the anxiety usually drops immediately, and you're learning that 'procrastinating makes me feel better,' forming a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite can undo it — doing it while anxious is effectively an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about what you should do, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better in the short term and worse in the long term, because you haven't solved the problem, you've just made yourself face it repeatedly later, or face worse consequences.

26:39 The burnout fix is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you're burned out because you're doing too much, doing things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take care of yourself more consciously — specifically, more deliberately deciding what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you're used to performing well, burnout makes your performance worse, so you work harder, then you burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this 'borrowing health and productivity from your future self.' He also notes burnout doesn't only come from hours: reasonable hours but high-pressure, meaningless, or otherwise draining tasks can also burn you out.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative in order to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings wholesale; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative in order to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings wholesale; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo lays out the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR and RLCD in fine detail, suited to anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without making a mistake, the model has to be extremely conservative, because errors are visible at a glance while the subtly wrong things that look correct are very hard to spot; this calibration is ‘total poison’ for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart showing that LLMs necessarily fail as sequences get longer is mathematically obvious but empirically false — when you cover the distribution you don't get over-penalized by outliers, and it's mode drop that throws away the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety problem
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is ‘doing what the user wants’, the former is ‘following someone else's instructions’, as with OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it is ‘nuts’ and ‘completely unacceptable’ — if a dependency is running in the background, having your software randomly crash because a user sent a strange message is insanity. He is against adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a little more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to pump up scores, which is essentially ‘benchmarking with extra steps’. He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if he wanted to make Jev dumb, he could have shipped that a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then it was learning to summarize, and only later did it become instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is ‘instruction following as the North Star’, with nothing to do with the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm and still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall, and the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's always some kind of reliability problem — it might be type safety, it might be determinism, or it might just be that the model is too jagged. He is explicitly against treating determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, holding that it is only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs getting similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says that when people get burned by AI decisions, that is exactly where it happens, at the robustness layer.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry has its attention in the wrong place: ‘people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability’. His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that is the mark of an economic revolution, and also what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all current models are still roughly at zero, maybe not even 1%, on valuable work in the world economy.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says outright that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not that ‘RLVR is useless’ but that the ‘pacing the frontier’ discussion smuggles in a premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model ‘do anything they want’ in the middle of training — the less you restrict it, the stronger the model is on the outside. So the danger is not a side effect, it is the design goal. He calls this a ‘disillusion of responsibility’: take ‘we must do more RLVR’ as an axiom, then derive the conclusion ‘we are heading toward a dangerous world’.

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents ‘free from the tyranny of the KV cache’. The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you have to keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction or decomposition, the normal practices of software. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents don't seem to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state around requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. The directions he envisions include explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context within a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

item.title: AI Will Hit an Energy Wall Within Three Years, and the Fix Is Building a Computer That Isn't a Computer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-allin-ai-三年内会撞上能源墙-解法是造一台不像计算机的计算机/
item.description: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month — at 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month — at 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public reveal of a physical dynamics computer prototype and measured efficiency numbers — rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month, and at the low-end figure of 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts. The US today puts about 40 gigawatts into data centers; the world is under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs — today it's energy. You secure the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; hardware capex and site come after.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts takes a GPU several watts
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt — exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, mice and bats are in the milliwatt range. A squirrel leaping between branches lands it a thousand times out of a thousand on 8 milliwatts of brain. Which is to say your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion is that biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, and synthetic systems took a different road: the human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second, while a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped, and the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still climbing, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped too, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen says flatly that Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital is itself an abstraction of the physical world, transistors actually have intermediate states and are engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network, skipping the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, and complex behavior emerges from the whole — the field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a board synchronize themselves
Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they will synchronize to exactly the same phase on their own, simply because each one gives the board a tiny push. That's a purely physical dynamical system. Their question was whether such a system can compute. The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and produces images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating a plane, a car or a bird follows a different state space trajectory. It's the first demonstration that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce useful results.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
Fully connected is n squared: 10 elements and 100 connections is fine, 1,000 elements is a million connections and simply doesn't scale. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some connections and seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds both in simulation and in real physical systems. Naveen calls this the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked for a long time, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already produced images
This is Naveen's first public reveal: they built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; they sent the design to tape-out on June 1, and the chip is already back in the lab and producing results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image takes about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoules for an ordinary GPU; a nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, several orders of magnitude apart. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it differs from both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann architectures with memory and compute separated, shuttling data back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call this 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions vertically and in-plane, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains are only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to hit the limit of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale mega data centers to small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price drop. Halve the price and consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth and consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then presses on the ecosystem question: tape-out, packaging and the rest require a whole set of people working together. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of an entire rack, sold as a new data center product — tokens in, tokens out over the network, but internally structured completely differently from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only about to reach diesel and prices.
item.content:encoded:
Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only about to reach diesel and prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil prices didn't rise" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The war began with Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply outright. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for every side. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral from there; it found several buffers that held prices down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — backup crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories refiners hold; levels were high before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a lot of Iranian and Russian "dark fleet" crude was floating at sea, and in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy it. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of global supply, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively leaving that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks slapped every analyst in the face
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and sentiment flipped 180 degrees instantly: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed weeks later, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this price contains a lot of bets on "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining, and the buffers are nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government only authorized a specific quantity. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized cap. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire this close
The Trump administration points to Venezuela as the solution, and its reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output you need to invest money, move rigs, hire people, drill, and ship the barrels out — that's a matter of years and billions of dollars. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to raise diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't seen prices spike at the pump yet; what's actually rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. So the question becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets to the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it, or pass it on
Businesses have only two choices. One is to hold the line on prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation Pennsylvania farmer, has raised his beef price only once in five years — even though the cost of hauling in hay is up 15% to 20%, he eats it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and holding out will be rewarded. A farmer's fuel exposure is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, shipping his own goods out — energy costs can be paid three times over. The other is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers raised straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions heated up again, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan commodity analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and nobody — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this lasts.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilizational variable and quantifies it — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't escape because it never learned escape
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped in a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not avoid no matter what it did; on day two it was put in a shuttle box where running to the other side would shut off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's judgment was that what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts shock" but "nothing I do matters." That reading collided head-on with behaviorism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones played a harsh noise, and for one group no amount of button-pressing could turn it off while for the other group pressing a button did. On day two came a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side and the noise sounds, move it to the other side and it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before just left their hand in the box. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature accumulated by then and found the lab could reproduce eight of them; the only one missing was thoughts of death — presumably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. The model went on to become the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up, one in three does not
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and about a third do not. From the 1970s on Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week predicts who drops out
The first six weeks at West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern showed up in college grades (optimists exceeded their talent, pessimists fell short of it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this group outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it later, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The Axial Age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BCE, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India, and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius, and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature, and the first political freedom erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad Achilles does not decide to act on his own, Athena tells him to act; a century later in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BCE every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament the verbs of divine command decline
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: roughly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further you go into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words of human agency appear and the fewer words of divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency, and plotted by time it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BCE, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom, and technology.

item.title: He Never Won Elected Office, Yet He Reshaped All of New York
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-stuffmissed-他从未当选任何公职-却重塑了整座纽约/
item.category: Stuff You Missed in History Class
item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions to accumulate power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions to accumulate power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode has medium information density, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the exact words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver in government to achieve goals without angering those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be made angry, and that a way had to be found to cut costs without cutting that many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green space plans simply preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — this is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned to build a large state park system for Long Island, all connected by new roads. In just four years in office, he added 13 parks to Long Island, about 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the media considered it impractical. He first used large-scale dredging to dig about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother Bella to continue the work. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have come back with the equipment to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting on Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried to run for office again, instead continuing to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Beginning in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
In 1945 Moses published an article in The Atlantic Monthly, opening with a description of how slums form: existing buildings overcrowded, speculators adding tenants, people packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums in most cities is done indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition-and-construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, lined with landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large amounts of land at a reasonable price had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain must be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly-wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘without rhyme or reason’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Blame Is Not Revenge: A Philosopher Argues We Should Blame Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.description: Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching a shared moral understanding.
item.content:encoded:
Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching a shared moral understanding.

In 23 minutes it offers a workable moral framework: distinguishing retributive from communicative blame, and explaining why blaming less does not mean giving up on responsibility.

0:04 There is no single definition of blame
Fricker points out that the philosophical literature holds a great many different views of blame: some say it is a hostile emotion, some a reactive attitude, some merely a judgment, some a rupture in a relationship, and some a form of protest. She suspects these views are not even talking about the same thing. She holds that the object of blame can be any agent — an individual, an institution, or even a collective as large as a nation — as long as it has done something wrong, it is a fitting object of blame.

2:05 Retributive blame has no logic to it
Fricker defines retributive blame as: you wronged me, I am at a disadvantage, so I am entitled to get even by making you hurt a little too — "evening the score" is its most apt metaphor. She says she does not believe this logic in interpersonal morality, and does not find it useful. She concedes she does not want to say anything specific about criminal punishment, but admits she is strongly inclined to think the retributive idea there is rather distasteful. She believes genuinely useful alternatives exist.

3:08 Communicative blame wants shared understanding
Fricker holds that the morally most valuable model of blame is the one aimed at getting the other person to fully grasp the moral significance of their conduct. If you blame me for wronging you, perhaps I did not fully understand the moral weight of what I did; you put it into the conversation, and I either come to understand what I did or push back that it was "not that serious," and in the end the two of us reach a shared moral understanding of what happened between us. She admits this is an ideal, but one worth pursuing, and calls it "communicative blame."

5:11 Blame is at bottom a judgment of moral wrongdoing
After the functional analysis, Fricker gives her definition of blame: blame is a judgment of moral wrongdoing, and that judgment is in some sense activated or motivated by a disposition suited to holding someone responsible. She stresses that this is the context of moral blame. The definition is minimalist, and she thinks its advantage is that it transplants across domains — when she studies epistemic blame, for instance, she need not assume the blamer harbours a hostile emotion toward the blamed; there need only be an epistemic fault, and a judgment made from a responsibility-holding stance rather than passive observation.

6:11 An apology must be made to the right person
Fricker points to a key difference between apology and blame: communicative blame can be spread around, and conveying the meaning of blame to a third party can be derived from conveying it to the person concerned — both promote shared moral understanding; but apologising to someone who is not the person you wronged is not an apology at all. Apology is essentially second-personal moral address, and must be done to the right person. She also notes that an apology's reparative power is tied to an ongoing relationship — if a stranger wrongs you at random, there is no need to chase an apology, and we all have to learn to let things go.

9:12 Sincerity is not all-or-nothing
Fricker disagrees with treating sincerity as all-or-nothing. She holds that in most apology practices, a person need only be "sincere enough" to count as apologising, and sincere enough in the right way to be accepted by the particular person being apologised to. She cites the philosopher Jeffrey Helmich's notion of the "apology stance": an apology is a speech act that not only expresses but "enacts" the appropriate sorry inner state. She adds that an over-elaborate apology is merely irritating, and that apology is a social performance that must fall within the bandwidth of appropriateness to be accepted.

12:15 Responsibility is a social construction, not metaphysics
Faced with the minority view that genes and environment determine everything and people are never responsible, Fricker argues that this line of thinking locates the threshold of responsibility in a metaphysical rather than a natural place. She understands responsibility as something that grows out of the practice of human beings living together, for the sake of social coordination and harmony and the construction of a shared moral consciousness. She borrows Peter Strawson's approach: whatever the metaphysics, in everyday life we simply cannot help praising and blaming. She holds that separating metaphysics from the practice of responsibility is itself a way of leading people astray.

19:20 Blaming less is a trainable choice
Fricker says that if blame is a judgment of fault, and the judgment comes from a responsibility-holding moral stance, then we can choose how much human behaviour to bring into this "fault-finding" construction. She gives the example of lateness: some people are highly moralistic about others being late, while others are not offended at all. She admits she prefers a world in which everyone is a little more relaxed about lateness of up to 15 minutes, where it need not be constructed as a matter of respect — it is just "you were a bit late," and that is all.
