item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap; the real reasons are release cadence and task focus, and US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a status briefing on open models written for Congress: high data density, clear judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same thing as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by non-profits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of the data it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss "open source," what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 achieved a step change in commercial viability, crossing an agentic capability threshold similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models passed the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, mainly on the back of Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion, twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, with a lower update cadence than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks such as physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use commonly, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely, for instance by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI, the gap from the strongest US models to Chinese open-weight models would only widen by 1-2 months. Distillation has the biggest effect in new domains, and cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs release faster and with a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs are continuously improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi, Airbnb uses Qwen, and Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to obtain product usage licenses, a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly processed tokens have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 they reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in autumn 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models see higher adoption at equal capability
Research shows that US models see disproportionately high adoption when capability and scale are comparable. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk requires ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, the ones hurt would be US companies. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the second half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in her study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school simply wasn't an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide dug tunnels without wet drilling and without giving workers protective gear, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing let more people know what happened, and connected people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is a pillar of democracy, not an illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains — all of it takes shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always stare at journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they may teach — that moves the same foundation. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry doesn't just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. You can judge whether a democracy is healthy by whether art can still live in an unfettered space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its uses aren't limited to poetry — you can use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that propaganda comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how someone is working on you is a good thing. And in America many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘aren't supposed to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem in a different person's voice, and you hear something different every time.

42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. There's an American saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behaviour of an entire people as a whole — that is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say — that itself is the capacity democracy needs.

47:58 Grief has to be put into language before you can hold it
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never imagined writing one or showing it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she isn't wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry, you throw away far more than you keep
She doesn't start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’ but from a word, an image, a phrase that is ringing there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when she has time to sit down she asks which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much do you write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage — keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’, the shape is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem; learning is not
She pushes back directly on the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She doesn't deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what's more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the loud repetition of the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing’. Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words out of the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and a crime for a free white person to teach them — what was being controlled was not the text but the people. So the sentence holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is taken away, there is only one logic: this is how you are easier to control.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward the pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward the pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain city-state of ancient Mesopotamia there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed enormous emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change the shape of politics
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way a book organises information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and critically analyse it. More crucially, the book limits the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to the Nazi elite, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extraordinarily powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote to each other and ran journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr elevates it enormously, even calling it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if a clever person sits alone in a village, his ideas can only be told to his neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into a central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — in conversation with Adam Smith, David Hume and Newton, the standard is naturally high; it is a kind of "submission to that which cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will engage with you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott argues there is a kind of truth about life that only prose fiction can reach: it lets us see the inside of another person's mind. Reading is an active, not a passive, process — you build images in your head out of the words on the page, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because what it gives you is the external world and it cannot enter another mind directly; writing, meanwhile, is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, mind communicating with mind. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to inhabit another mind appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, holding that great film can approach it through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity that is conveyed by more than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator does not explain and analyse the world like the print-age public intellectual, but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable tales for a captivated audience. Roberts calls this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them with the author's standard — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that captivates. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds on reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: Jagger's "Sympathy for the Devil" opens by taking directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel begins with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and belief, after which a suave gentleman appears, they take him for mad, and finally realise he is Satan. Marriott calls it an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you have to move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have grown less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours simplicity and immediacy: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see whether it holds up — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from the analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport so I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not new particles, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but never converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water that the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is that all these perspectives are real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘ultimate glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

6:13 We still have not digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is a huge revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirmed what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we still do not really believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of an observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the reality at the most basic level physics can reach is not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry or James's characters deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard, it has just not been digested; the specific physical phenomena are of course complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and piecing a new concept out of the parts. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain better understanding, better ways of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective is not the same as saying all perspectives are equal, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is ‘what is a good life’.

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, a poet has to learn too. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, poets and poems are probably very good at that, but that is not what difficulty means’. She gives the example of poems on the underground: before everyone looked at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem, and that engagement was far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised ‘efficiency’ and stripped out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — ‘this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — and his reaction is ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read’. He connects this back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September and statements by the UN Secretary-General and the Pope to connect the argument about perspectives to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in hypocritical narratives — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford immediately offers a counterexample: we also always need simplicity, and if we embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day we might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people how to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet sits on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the entire event introduced no new AI feature; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet sits on the foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is willingness to make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by offering a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision, it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he has a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two men from talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 but rolled out no notable new AI features, and the roughly 15-minute opening just retold the Apple Intelligence story of the past two years. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution, one that spans the globe and is enormous, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's read on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple took five years to replace the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of the handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top brass either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up the order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand the baton to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you never want to leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept with a title invented on the spot
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right in the middle of the preparations for Ternus to take over. Cook got him to stay and take part in the transition, and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement, and that the man already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, ditched Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on modems, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that ‘we never owned search, we don't need to own AI’. He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own a cellular modem that had already been commoditised, buying and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem but unwilling to own AI is ridiculous. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is pushing its own models again, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers high salaries.

48:53 The watch's always-on transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's always-on listening feature was ‘I can't believe they did it’. The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs some degree of ambient capture, but the societal privacy problem is unsolved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now they're 85%, and within five or six years they were past half; the iPhone itself wasn't the source of that, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting at a future combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
