The host says she once believed that without punishments and consequences children would run wild — she even stood in the shower when her daughter was four months old thinking ‘how do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom.’ Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had treated ‘obedience’ as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, recording for the host to see, she deliberately didn't threaten, punish, or reward — she just asked her two-year-old son ‘why don't you want to brush your teeth,’ and he couldn't put it into words; he just called out ‘Mama’ and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and they sang a song together — and he brushed his teeth himself, the whole thing in under five minutes.

21:31 ‘I need you to take out the trash’ is not a need
The host says that looking back, she didn't understand what a ‘need’ was — she thought saying ‘I need you to take out the trash’ to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born the two of them almost never argued: mountain biking in summer, skiing in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid them in vouchers. After their daughter was born everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave her husband would fetch her anything she wanted, and the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for ‘collaboration, partnership, effort being seen’ that actually pried open the problems between them; before that she was carrying a large amount of resentment inside her with no idea how to handle it.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted — the moment her husband interrupts her she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage a package needed. She always assumed the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he stopped, everything would be fine. Recording in July 2018 with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it live to her own father, a special education teacher who would treat sixteen-year-olds like ten-year-olds and who, for a stretch, lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said ‘Don't interrupt me, Mama,’ and her husband looked at her and said ‘She is you.’ She says that was the moment she realized this had never just been about the two people in the room, and out of it she developed the ‘Tame Your Triggers’ course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, the word ‘me’ cut out of the board on one cover and ‘you’ embossed on the other when you flipped it over — the concept being ‘you came out of me.’ On the ‘me’ side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the ‘you’ side she wrote to Carys, whom she had not yet met. She reads out the earliest batch of ‘expectations for you’: I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands with people instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you pick yourself up and say ‘I'm fine.’ She says looking back, her biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person and let them be their whole self and witness that, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once assumed she would play the role of ‘enforcer,’ and even wrote ‘I hope you can love me the way I love him’ on her pregnancy expectations list. She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what actually planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: principle two is to reconsider your demands — ‘maybe when a child won't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child but the thing you're asking’; principle five is to change the way you look, not just the way you act — when you see your child do the thing you asked them not to do, your first reaction is curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; principle ten is ‘attribute to your child the best motive consistent with the observed facts,’ and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to ‘consistent with the observed behavior,’ because ‘there are no facts, only what we observe.’

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject, it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things — when she started the parenting membership eight years ago she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module, because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy, because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin she had been together ten years and had never learned how to disagree, because most of that time was spent doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same work she'd been doing with her child all these years — while also believing the Gottman method itself has a few key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools, and one couple — where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue — found that after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, he was willing to talk, and in that same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was flagged as bots. It was actually a group of middle schoolers.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had blocked social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four independent stories, medium information density, but the generational misreading in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments weren't bots, they were kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible messages in the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, assumed bots, and reported and deleted them. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are children. Her evidence was the display names with emoji you need a special character generator to type, cartoon avatars she'd never seen, and a way of talking that was short back-and-forth sentences plus lots of exclamation points. Dave wasn't buying it at first, and replied, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as the entry point to a group chat
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids did it: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with a single podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also posted Google Forms as quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That was the detail that convinced Dave.

8:06 They picked NPR because nobody was in the comments
The team reached out to several commenters, and only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed; she did it from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core group was about 20 kids, many of them in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who wouldn't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started using playlists to move to new ground. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get pulled into other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that the episode made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he was. Ella said she was sure that one day she too would be as completely lost as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the whole episode's theme of "intergenerational space travel."

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody heard
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last, moves to the mother standing by the counter smoking, and then turns at the end toward "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with that dark a picture on her wedding day would indeed make it hard to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother had a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: the mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she bought the wedding dress, that she wasn't that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. The exchange turns all the earlier argument about the wedding toast into a question about why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Getting rid of the stepfather is what repaired them
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and get Mr. X out. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she'd ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that, that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart, and getting rid of him pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the entry point to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and one day she blurted out, "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then immediately realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, but her mother said: braiding shouldn't be the entry point for making a child tough, because it carries too much racial and gender meaning; and besides, six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of her own hair, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Robots Are Still at the GPT-1 Stage — the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.description: The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss doesn't mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
item.content:encoded:
The Scaling Law signal for embodied intelligence has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss doesn't mean high success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.

Xu Mengdi (徐梦迪), assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning for embodied intelligence. The middle-to-late section on the data flywheel and the loss trap is the most valuable part.

12:15 Pretraining isn't everything — adaptation is
Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is titled Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you can't hope a robot will succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — a home has 20 objects today, a week later it has 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences shift too. So a robot must be able to adapt to change in its deployment environment and improve itself there. She explored two routes: In-Context Learning and test-time training, the latter changing only 0.5% of the adapter parameters — but change too many and it forgets the pretrained knowledge.

19:22 Why adaptation only started to matter now
Humans generalise well for two reasons: an extremely strong prior, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — in effect, giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this doesn't mean adaptation is unimportant — it's just that people only recently realised it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

49:46 Low loss doesn't mean high success rate
This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There's a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate isn't necessarily low — there's a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object at all. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if step 18 — the first real contact with the object — has a relatively large error, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

50:47 Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to reach is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, with no fine-tuning needed — telling the model what to do purely through context. That way fine-tuning's share drops even lower, it's easier to scale to more scenarios and complete more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

58:49 The data flywheel is a chicken-and-egg problem
The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data flywheel. That requires putting the robot into end-user homes or service scenarios, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot showing obvious progress after half an hour of teaching — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then does the data flywheel start turning. But there's a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, which is what draws out the base capability. So whether the data flywheel can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

1:03:52 Data is defined backwards from model capability
Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data isn't conjured out of thin air — it's defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they're actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model needs, and working backwards to how the data should be collected. If you need smoother motion, the data has to be of the smooth kind; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data has to be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now people's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

1:05:54 Each of the four data types has its place
Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalisation and texture generalisation, making the model more robust to visual change, and suits the front end of pretraining or mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle — more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scene variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

1:19:02 AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
Robotics papers have been doubling recently, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar while in fact many arguments are full of holes and there isn't much content. If she finds out an article was AI-written, her interest in it is discounted.

item.title: The woman who killed Marat, and why the court wouldn't believe she acted alone
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.description: Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone — yet the revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy." They could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.
item.content:encoded:
Corday had her declaration written before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone — yet the revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her on the "chain of conspiracy." They could not imagine that provincials thought Marat a monster.

High information density: it threads the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain, and the back half on the assassination details is especially valuable.

0:00 The assassination declaration was written before the act
When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile of scoundrels," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and is therefore outside the law," and called on the French to "rise. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc defense — it was written before the act. What she wanted was not escape, but to turn her own death into a rallying point.

9:30 Marat was the first modern populist
Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His recipe included: ceaselessly invoking the capitalized "People," and claiming the people were at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theory, openly stating that his goal was to keep his readers "perpetually on their guard," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and their ilk. The show points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used today by both left and right.

21:57 Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
In early 1793 France had suffered years of poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government had no money to fight its wars, so it printed paper money — the assignat — with roughly four billion in circulation. This triggered severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, protests broke out in the markets almost daily, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The show stresses: these were the very same conditions that had set off the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "the Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

32:13 The commander-in-chief's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counterattacked and routed Dumouriez at Neerwinden; he was forced to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, and asked his troops, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking a group of senior officers with him, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. One volunteer wrote to his mother: "Who can we trust now?"

38:27 The Terror machine was improvised, not planned
The show stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint and no plan — they were built as they went, and only in hindsight did they assemble into a machine, and many of those who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal; it sat in the Palais de Justice in Paris, and its cellars were the existing Conciergerie prison. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

42:37 The Girondins used a new rule to strike at Marat, and it backfired
Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins took advantage of the many deputies away on missions to the provinces and, on 14 April, brought an indictment against Marat, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat hid for three days, then found that street opinion in Paris was on his side and simply turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the court convened in the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and let Marat deliver a long defense. The ten-man jury acquitted him within a few hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by some 800 people, crowned with roses, with cries of "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

1:04:31 Corday bought a knife: a 15-centimetre kitchen knife with a black handle
At around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the arcades of the Palais-Royal, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing the white Norman-style hat that marked her as a provincial. She went into a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 centimetres long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but she had no appointment and was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

1:10:51 The court wouldn't believe a woman could act alone
Corday was arrested on the spot, and one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognized Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must have been part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: it's impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the man who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators — so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you're mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in the other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that provincials would think Marat a bad man.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete history of a storage technology's failure, from RMM in 1970 to the Optane shutdown in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change memory is what makes it slow
Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between its crystalline and amorphous states: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and then cools it slowly so it crystallises, or heats it to a temperature high enough to turn it crystalline without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behaviour of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot about it
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory", positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing data that programs read often but rarely change. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later, when someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan as well. NOR did not have NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stored boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% of power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling reason to exist was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, going their separate ways after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND for them. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel switched to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into a single volatile memory pool, working out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database normally takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel gave an update on Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not part of the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane had only a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilised capacity and dragged $400 million a year off the company; the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realise that it was not just CPUs that needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit badly weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was a proprietary technology. In July 2022, on its earnings call, Intel quietly announced it was shutting down the Optane business.

item.title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: not compatible with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.description: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a choke point but instead goes proactively into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.
item.content:encoded:
For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that does not solve a choke point but instead goes proactively into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder the longer you do it.

The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's project launch onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of frontline detail and judgment that only appear in the book.

16:10 Ascend's toughest decision was not being compatible with Nvidia
At project launch Ascend faced two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has proven correct today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they must take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice was extremely bold at the time, and that they faced enormous challenges many times along the way — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed based on its own root technologies.

19:11 Anything you do as a follower gets harder and harder
Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half-muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets harder and harder. There are two kinds of following: in standardized products, Chinese companies can always catch up and even overtake, but by the time they overtake there is little profit left in the industry — 2G to 5G, PCs, phones all went this way; in non-standardized areas, such as competing with Cisco in routers for so many years, they have not gotten closer. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve choke points and address survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

29:16 With process choked off, only system innovation can make it back
Industry chips gain roughly 20%+ performance per generation, mainly from increased transistor counts driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost this premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong uses a car metaphor: previously you just made the engine stronger and stronger, but now the engine is constrained and cannot be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction, heat dissipation and other factors. Nvidia's solution is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture for it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies are good at only one layer because of the great division of labor, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

34:21 Huawei has to bring the domestic supply chain up with it
Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, directly buy American products and assemble them, sell at a good price with brand premium and decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and drive the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also driving the entire supply chain — without driving it, independent autonomy is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory continuously advance process, yield and quality.

37:40 Ascend's significance is not Huawei surviving, but the industry having an engine
In the past Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and industrial ecosystem; the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, drive almost 100% domestic supply chains. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be autonomous, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, looking at reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point — when Nvidia is mentioned people think it is formidable, when Huawei is mentioned they say it is policy that makes people use it.

45:47 It is not a question of difficulty, but of cognition and determination
Fang Xingdong believes doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and determination — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the Gauss database: among the six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous may be Gauss, but databases are a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and if truly choked it would be deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support domestic vendors, but after research found none were up to the task; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks of American giants, with small scale, weak R&D and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, investing 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year starting in 2011 and 2012, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

1:06:04 The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
Fang Xingdong judges that global high tech moving from a single US-centered system to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company, every country, big or small, have a choice and not be forced to pick one side under coercion. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; it is not a simple substitution relationship with Nvidia but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and co-opetition. He admits the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced processes are also broken through, it can pursue both tracks at once.

1:19:11 The tech war won short term, but the long-term cost is greater
Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might be at least one-third of Nvidia, one-third of Apple, possibly China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly exceeded Samsung's for one quarter. Nvidia today is dominant; if it had been running neck and neck with Huawei in AI chips from the start, it could not have reached this position. He judges that once the attacked party builds a self-circulation that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning from a monopoly into two competitors.

item.title: Ads Are Machine Learning 1.0: How AppLovin Earned an 84% Margin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-allin-广告是机器学习的-1-0-applovin-靠它赚出-84-利润率/
item.description: Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising isn't AI's past tense — it's the earliest and most profitable deployment of deep learning. AppLovin used recommendation models to build an 84% EBITDA margin in the $50 billion mobile game ad market, and became its own best investor with $6 billion in buybacks.

A CEO who almost never gives interviews explains the shared technical roots of advertising and AI, the buyback playbook through a 92% drawdown, and why a Chinese engineering team is an advantage. High information density, worth listening to.

1:02 Mobile game advertising is a $50 billion market
Adam says outsiders underestimate the scale of mobile gaming: more than a billion adults play casual mobile games every day, and these people are household decision-makers. Two years ago AppLovin disclosed $11 billion in annual ad spend on its own platform, and it has grown roughly 60% year over year since, which by rough math puts it around $20 billion today. But that isn't the whole market — many other ad companies are monetizing in this ecosystem, so double that number and the entire mobile game ecosystem spends roughly $50 billion a year on advertising. He notes that not long ago social was also just a $50 billion opportunity.

3:02 Advertising is machine learning's earliest and most profitable implementation
Adam calls advertising ML 1.0: it was the first deployment of all the technology that now drives AI. Large language models create more economic value today than advertising, but advertising is an extremely profitable implementation of deep learning models. Recommendation systems and large language models differ in structure, but their trajectories are highly similar — research in large language models can transfer to recommendation systems and vice versa; many large language model researchers spent the early part of their careers looking at ad systems. The beauty of the ad business is that you build a model to predict a future outcome, and the value of that prediction can be converted into money immediately.

6:03 Search advertising creates no economic increment; discovery does
Adam splits advertising into two categories. One is bottom-of-funnel advertising: the consumer already knows what they want to buy and is just doing research to complete the transaction — that's Google Search's business, and large language models will compete with Google Search almost entirely in that domain. The other is where he operates: not knowing user intent, creating a demand that didn't previously exist, so the user sees something and thinks ‘this looks really cool, I want to buy it right now’. He stresses that the transaction in search or in a large language model was going to happen anyway, so there isn't much economic expansion there; discovery advertising creates economic increment, which is what makes Meta's ad business strong and what AppLovin wants to do.

8:07 Your phone isn't listening, but your behavior is tracked
Faced with the question of ‘I mention something at lunch and then an ad shows up’, Adam says it's more likely you took a trackable action earlier — a search, a website visit, a product search — without realizing it, and then you said something related and started seeing related ads. He states plainly that AppLovin does not track location at all, arguing that tracking precise location to render ads is a very heavy concept, and that the data transfer required to parse microphone content in real time and translate it into ads isn't realistic. But he concedes that if you're on a social network, relationship data between you and others can of course drive the ad experience — for instance, a friend searched for something and you might see a related ad, which he thinks is fine.

10:07 From $28 billion to $3.8 billion, then it started buying itself
AppLovin went public in April 2021 with $600 million in EBITDA at a market cap of about $28 billion, peaking at $40 billion. In 2022 the stock fell almost every day, down to a market cap of about $3.8 billion — in a year when the company did $1 billion in EBITDA. Adam's read: market cap is determined by the quality of your investors, and at the time a huge number of companies were going public at once, so blue-chip investors hadn't done the research to figure out what this company with the silly name was. The result was no demand and lots of supply, and the valuation fell from 50x EBITDA to under 4x. His response was to stop talking to investors and instead use the large amounts of cash the company generated to buy back aggressively; since then it has bought roughly $6 billion of its own stock and retired 20% to 25% of shares outstanding.

12:07 When the stock is down 92%, family call to ask if you're suicidal
Adam says that period was hard — family and friends would call to ask if he was suicidal, and his answer was that the stock was still at $10 and had still gone up a lot. But the truly hard part was realizing that as CEO, his team was getting the same calls, and they didn't have his composure or his equity. So they rallied the team around a ‘we versus the world’ mentality, and extended a performance stock program usually reserved for the CEO to key people across the company, telling them: it's hard right now, the house you thought you had is gone, but if you hold on and recover, the upside is enormous. Later investors started coming back, the company switched from regression models to deep learning models, the ad algorithms got better, advertiser returns got better, and the business started growing fast.

14:08 One week in New York, market cap went from $28 billion to $55 billion
When the new model launched in April 2023 the company still wasn't talking to investors, so the outside world didn't know. By around September 2023 the stock was at $80 with good results, and Adam judged the market cap high enough that it couldn't buy back that aggressively anymore, so he went to New York and started talking to investors. In that one week the stock went from $80 to $150 and the market cap went from $28 billion to $55 billion — just because he went out and said ‘our company is still here, we survived’. He describes sitting in meetings and being able to read that the person across the table was texting a friend to buy. Over the next two and a half years the stock went from $9 to $750, a $250 billion market cap. His conclusion is that public market investors and private investors aren't that different — they all chase trends, just often later than you'd like.

16:09 After privacy rules tightened, users complained ads got worse
Adam says in these areas you want regulatory clarity, and once the rules are clear, technology can respond. Five years ago you could target users precisely on iOS; today if users say no precise targeting, you can only bundle them into groups and serve worse ads. The interesting result of that change was that after Apple's changes the company received a flood of user complaints saying ‘show me more relevant ads, you're showing me a bunch of junk now’. So he offers a two-sided view: on one hand you need privacy regulation so tech companies know what to do, and on the other consumers genuinely want relevant ads — when you watch a 30-second ad in a game to get an extra life, you're getting something with monetary value, and you don't want to spend those 30 seconds on junk.

item.title: Buffets Weren't Eaten Out of Business — They Were Hollowed Out by the Supermarket Deli
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-modernmba-自助餐不是被吃垮的-是被超市熟食区掏空的/
item.description: The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap ingredients, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.
item.content:encoded:
The 1980s buffet was propped up by cheap ingredients, cheap land, cheap labor and stagnant wages. When all four inputs got more expensive, what actually killed it was the supermarket deli eating the low-price market at zero customer-acquisition cost.

It dissects an industry's cause of death using three public companies' financials and bankruptcy filings — the mechanism is clear and the numbers are solid, and the back half on supermarket deli counters is the most valuable part.

0:02 The buffet deleted everything hard about running a restaurant
The real leap of the 1980s buffet was upgrading "unlimited" from a side dish to the entire business model. It cut every hard part of a traditional restaurant: no servers to hire, no menu to design, almost no English required, no precision needed. The only job was cooking in bulk, heating frozen appetizers, and slicing factory cake into portions. Compared with a regular restaurant where every dish has to earn back its own price, a buffet only has to keep the trays full. Lower skill threshold, a concept that sells itself, one family able to run the whole kitchen, customers serving themselves — the whole model ran on volume. Within a decade, nearly every small town in the Midwest had a Chinese buffet.

8:07 Opening restaurants and keeping customers are two different businesses
Buffets Inc.'s Old Country and Hometown had the simplest strategy: this model doesn't need improvement, it needs replication. From one location to 200 in a decade, doubling again in five years, at its peak opening more than one a week, and after the 1996 merger the largest and fastest buffet operator in the world, with annual revenue near a billion dollars. But fast success created a fatal blind spot — they built the muscle for opening buffets, not the muscle for keeping customers. Neither chain had a real brand, a signature dish, or a trademarked recipe; they competed only on price and on volume of advertising rather than quality. The company bet everything on "scale itself compounds," and 17% restaurant-level margins in the early 1990s meant nobody dared question the playbook.

9:07 Same-store sales fell for five straight years and nobody knew why
In 1994 same-store sales turned negative and stayed red for five consecutive years; sales stagnated for over a decade, trailing inflation. Nothing about the restaurants themselves had changed: nearly 40% of both chains' locations had been opened or remodeled in the past two years, price increases were small, and after the merger there was no competitor left. But customers simply stopped coming, as if Americans had suddenly had enough starting in the mid-1990s, and the format and the chains' novelty inexplicably wore off. The company tried fix after fix, all of them one-year band-aids: in 1995 it cut advertising below 1% of sales to buy profit, and the next year posted the worst same-store sales in its history; only tripling the ad budget turned same-store sales positive — meaning it had to keep marketing and sacrifice margin just to get people through the door.

11:07 Six years under private equity and traffic never improved once
In 2000 a New York private equity firm borrowed over $500 million to take Buffets Inc. private, and the spreadsheet logic was beautiful: cut costs, maximize earnings, cover the acquisition debt's interest with cash flow, squeeze the remaining customers dry, then repackage it for an IPO. But over the six-year holding period traffic never improved. The firm immediately raised prices, cut staff and service, then compensated with promotions, which only alienated customers further and eroded margin. By 2005 the once-healthy company was stuffed with debt, the firm had taken a $90 million dividend for itself, and what was left was a shell paying lenders more interest than the restaurants earned. Buying Ryan's was just a bigger dose of the same disease — the money came from selling off the land under most of Ryan's restaurants, turning the only asset that didn't depend on traffic into a new annual rent bill.

15:09 No meat was Fresh Choice's profit itself
Fresh Choice tried to solve the economics from the other end: replace expensive protein, which drives up food cost, with cheap salad and carbs. It charged the same prices in Northern California as Old Country and Hometown did in Ohio, while its food cost stayed 10% below its competitors' — that gap was the entire profit. But customers consistently refused to pay more without a real main course, and every investment meant to justify a price increase only accelerated the churn. The company couldn't give in either, because "no meat" was precisely where its profit came from. It tried uniform pricing, ending discounts, adding chicken to the salad, launching thicker soups, designing smaller and cheaper new store formats — none of it worked. By the late 1990s, falling traffic plus a complete lack of pricing power dragged the company into annual losses and penny-stock territory.

21:14 Even the most efficient operator went down all the same
Sweet Tomatoes was the most efficient, most disciplined operator in the industry, and it still came apart. From the start it built itself as a destination: standalone restaurants with private parking on land it owned, rather than renting in strip malls like its rivals. Each store had a 55-foot salad bar, eight made-from-scratch soups, a baked potato bar, a dessert bar, a pasta station and a bakery, and from the 1980s it pushed signature items like tuna tarragon and Joan's broccoli madness, branded dishes that injected crucial credibility. For sites it picked business districts and near shopping centers that could capture both lunch and dinner, buying land where it could and otherwise locking in 30-year leases. It also centralized on both the prep and store sides, building 19 central kitchens to make food in bulk and distribute it to each store, and when expanding it placed new stores near central kitchens to keep capacity utilization up. But logic and discipline only delayed the inevitable.

24:14 What killed the buffet was the supermarket deli counter
The way all three giants died was no coincidence: Fresh Choice had the cheapest food cost and died because customers wouldn't pay more than $7 for dinner; Sweet Tomatoes was the most efficient operator and survived as long as it did only because it owned the land under its restaurants; Buffets Inc. had the most locations, the cheapest labor and the strongest economies of scale, and still couldn't raise prices without losing customers. And the fast food and casual chains that had hitched a ride in the 1980s reached the conclusion first — by the late 1990s Wendy's, Burger King and KFC had all shut down their salad bars and unlimited bundles, because none of them made money. The real killer came from inside the supermarket: frozen meals failed to disrupt the buffet because they're single-serving while the buffet is designed for families; but dinner just moved to the deli counter of that same supermarket. The supermarket doesn't need the deli to support the whole store, prices by the pound and by the piece, and customers already came in weekly for milk and eggs — the deli is a cross-sell at zero customer-acquisition cost that also shares labor and overhead.

30:22 Not one of the buffet's four profit levers could be pulled
Every restaurant has only four levers to profit: raise prices, shrink portions, cut labor, shrink the footprint. The buffet chains had none of them. They couldn't raise prices, couldn't cut labor, couldn't shrink portions, couldn't shrink the restaurant. Since the 1990s the whole restaurant industry has moved toward "do more in less space," but a buffet can never truly be efficient — it needs those square feet to hold the variety that makes it appealing, and once it goes big it has to stay big. That worked in the 1980s, when land was cheap, malls were sprouting everywhere, and landlords cared more about traffic than rent. But as malls fell out of favor, retail migrated, and e-commerce hollowed out the strip centers, these chains found themselves locked into 10,000-square-foot boxes nobody wanted. That's why all the chains filed Chapter 11 over and over — bankruptcy was the only legal way to shed hundreds of leases nobody would take over.

item.title: More Collaboration, Slower System: The Counterintuitive Management Playbook from the Product Chiefs at Snap and Discord
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-lennys-协作越多越慢-snap-和-discord-产品一号位反直觉管理法/
item.description: Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately internalizes collaboration costs aggressively, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.
item.content:encoded:
Collaboration has hidden costs nobody has internalized, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So Peter Sellis deliberately internalizes collaboration costs aggressively, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better.

High information density, but the second half is worth more than the first. For people who want to hear how a product leader actually makes decisions, not for people who want specific growth playbooks.

6:07 More collaboration makes the system slower
Peter says you will never hear an executive say ‘stop collaborating’, and to him that is precisely a warning sign. Collaboration brings enormous coordination costs, and coordination costs guarantee you can only move as fast as the slowest node in the system. So he deliberately and aggressively internalizes collaboration costs, rather than defaulting to more collaboration being better. This is also where his ‘design teams like a terrorist organization’ comes from: one ideological culture that makes everyone understand why you are doing this thing, plus a very clear organizational structure specifying who can be trusted to make which decision. With those two things, you don't need to over-collaborate and you still get results that feel like you collaborated.

16:12 The median PM gap is a mathematical structure problem
Peter offers a distributional explanation: product management ability is normally distributed in the population, and the people who actually become PMs are cut from the right tail; once you cut it, it becomes a power-law distribution, and the median of a power-law distribution is far below the mean. Layer on two more mechanisms: in the ZERP era it became the most lucrative career in tech for people without a technical background, and the definition is subjective, so the people who get in have extremely strong incentives to stay; meanwhile the genuinely strong ones have skills that map almost perfectly onto other executive roles or starting their own company, so ‘great product managers are exiting the system’. Squeezed from both ends, the median is naturally bad. He also points out that the people actually complaining about PMs are the middle cohort of engineers — great engineers know how to bend a PM into the shape they want, and terrible engineers can hide behind the PM's decisions.

21:16 Snap's ad business can't scale for three mathematical reasons
First, users are extremely young, and between 17 and 18, and between 18 and 21, there is a ‘suspicious discontinuity’ in ad CPMs in and outside the US; the rules for tracking, measuring and targeting under-17s are extremely strict, and what is hard to measure is hard to build performance products around. Second, almost all non-search display advertising opens on a screen that shows ads, whereas Snap opens a camera — in the core flow of taking a snap and sending it to a friend, there is no logical place to put an ad; it is a creation-oriented rather than consumption-oriented product. Third, it is fundamentally a messaging app, and there is currently no good messaging ad product; Asian chat apps get cited over and over, but break it down by dollars spent per unit of time and none of them does particularly well.

35:25 Taste is the nerve to leave good things on the shelf
Peter says one thing he learned at Snap: he watched Evan say no to better ideas than almost anything any other consumer startup has ever shipped. He describes the product leader's goal as turning the founder into the world's richest museum curator — what is currently on display in the product is only a small part of the whole collection, the pieces the curator judged right for this time and place. He offers an interview technique for probing taste: ask what the person built but never shipped — not something killed because the data was bad, but something they held as a prototype and then judged ‘the world isn't ready’ or ‘this thing isn't ready’. If a museum hung its entire collection on the walls, the curator would have done nothing.

40:29 Advertising is the internet's product-market fit
Peter comes down squarely on Eric Seufert's side: advertising is the internet's product-market fit, and subscription consumer products are overrated. He judges OpenAI to have ‘last mover advantage’ in ads — Meta already solved modern ad auctions, this ‘solved problem’, from 2010 to 2020, and OpenAI is just running through each component quickly. Mechanically he names the modified VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves) auction: it isn't the highest bidder who wins, but rather the advertiser's natural value for that user is folded into the bid, so whoever bids high has to pay more to reach people who don't want to be reached. This mechanism lets organic content and ad content sit in the same auction, with dollars as the common denominator.

42:30 In chat, the denominator for ads is trust, not relevance
Peter replaces ‘natural value’ in VCG with ‘trust’ in the chat context. A user asks ‘which microphone should I buy’, and the product has to decide whether to give an objective answer, a set of answers, or an advertiser-influenced answer — and the degree of influence should equal how much trust you are willing to trade away. He uses Amazon search as an example: search for something and you scroll past 16 ads before the first real result, which subtly erodes users' trust in the system. So OpenAI's real deciding factor isn't whether to do ads, but how to mathematically maximize long-term trust inside the auction mechanism — trust maximization is probably correlated with retention, and may even be causal.

50:35 Growth comes from the core, not from new markets
Verified twice at Snap and Discord: a network-effects business wants to grow on its own, and the most effective move is to serve better — faster, more relevantly — the people already using the product, or wanting to use it, for the thing it is actually for. He explains with eighth-grade math: it takes 30 monthly actives to equal one daily active, so consumer products should optimize the DAU/MAU ratio; moving that ratio a few basis points is far more worthwhile than pulling in a pile of new MAUs and gambling on retention. Snap's lesson came from the disastrous 2018 redesign, the only quarter Snap's overall DAU went flat quarter over quarter; after that the team ground away at Android performance, producing a multi-year growth revival. Discord's version is more counterintuitive: at the time Midjourney was built on Discord, and outsiders all thought this was Discord's big opportunity, but Peter says if you pull up the Discord usage curve, you simply cannot pick out the Midjourney segment.

1:02:44 SpaceX is burning its own ships by hand
Peter considers SpaceX the greatest company right now, and the most worth learning from is how it fights the future: Falcon 9 is the world's best reusable launch system, other countries would trade GDP for it, and yet SpaceX announced it will stop selling Falcon 9 seats in a few years and pivot to Starship. He calls it a Cortez-level burning of the ships, a way to avoid what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma — because even holding the best thing, you are still willing to build the thing that makes your current product irrelevant. He also notes that SpaceX and Tesla publish their ten-year plans openly on their websites, and Tesla even open-sources its patents; that confidence — ‘I'll tell you what to do, and if you think you can do it better, come copy it’ — is what he aspires to as a product leader.

item.title: Paying Hip-Hop's Pioneers What They're Owed, and They Thought It Was a Scam
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-a16z-给嘻哈元老发钱-他们以为是诈骗/
item.description: Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. Because handing out cash directly doesn't work in hip-hop — Nas's take is that you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.
item.content:encoded:
Some didn't even show up to collect, because they didn't believe it was real. Because handing out cash directly doesn't work in hip-hop — Nas's take is that you have to give recognition and dignity first, and only then can the money be accepted.

This isn't an investment interview, it's a roundtable on how to pay back a debt owed to a culture. Worth listening if you care about distribution mechanisms in the creator economy, or want to know what Ben Horowitz is actually busy with in private.

2:04 A $10 album owed $5 million
The starting point is a debt Ben Horowitz owed himself: he bought the album Paid in Full for $10 back then, and over his career he got at least $5 million of value out of that record, with no channel to pay it back — and he felt he had to. He called Steve Stoute first, and Steve said the idea wasn't just good but timely — everyone was saying these old rappers were broke and dusty, but nobody was actually doing anything. The second call went to Nas, who said Quincy Jones's Jazz Foundation model wouldn't work in hip-hop: you can't just give a person money, it has to be recognition of what he did and who he is, and it has to be more than money. So the shape became an awards ceremony and a Grandmaster Award, with the first class honoring Scarface and Rakim.

5:05 Some thought it was a scam and didn't come collect
The foundation's first obstacle wasn't money, it was that nobody believed it. Ben says the level of disbelief early on exceeded imagination, and for a while they even had a hard time actually getting the money into people's hands — some didn't even show up to accept the award because they thought it was a scam, and others said "I don't need someone giving me money." He treats that disbelief as evidence the design was right: it can't look like compensation, it has to be celebration and tribute, shining the light they deserve on them, and only then will it be accepted. Caz later put it more bluntly: the industry has shortchanged these people for so long that the first reaction can only be "why would anyone help us now."

10:07 The first hip-hop hit was stolen from him
Grandmaster Caz wrote the rhyme that became Rapper's Delight, his name was even in the rhyme, and the first hip-hop hit was taken out of his hands just like that, and he never got what he was owed. Ben says everyone in the music industry knows this, but nobody has ever done anything, and nobody has ever said anything. The first time he met Caz in New York he was stunned: this is a person who changes the energy of any room he walks into today, and yet there's not a trace of bitterness on him, he still treats himself as a star. Steve added: it's not that nobody knows, it's that not enough people know — the industry knows, the public doesn't.

17:10 Dr. Dre asked for an introduction to his idol
Steve Stoute told a detail: Dr. Dre decided to come after hearing about Paid in Full, then asked him whether he could introduce him to Kool Moe Dee — Dre had never met him. Another time in Las Vegas, Dre again asked whether he could introduce him to Slick Rick, whom he'd also never met. A Dre who has made it asking someone for an introduction just to meet these legends shows how fragmented the scene is, and getting these people into one room was something only this foundation managed to do. Caz put it more directly: the industry separates people by success, status, who's hot right now; for years he only ran into Nas by chance, and now they see each other once a year and can call each other.

32:20 The Grammys botched it, so they did it themselves
Quincy Jones was the legend of legends to this group, but when he died the Grammy tribute was called out flatly as "botched." The Quincy Jones Award wasn't about inventing a category — it came from seeing the Grammys get it wrong, and Quincy's son QD3 saying then let's do it ourselves, and only then did it become a fixed annual award from the foundation. This year's recipient is Nile Rodgers. Steve mentioned that George Clinton showed up last year, brought his "mothership" prop, and at 83 recited the lyrics to Rakim's Follow the Leader on stage — a man who changed music, paying tribute to another man who changed music.

39:24 Hip-hop has no social security
Caz explained what this money concretely means: it's a grant paid out over five years, and he bought a house and moved out of the projects. He lived in the Bronx his whole life, and for the past ten to fifteen years his last thought in his head was always "I don't want to die in the projects," and now he and his wife live in a house in Pennsylvania. He says hip-hop has no social security, no health insurance, you have to keep working, so the reason you see him still doing radio, park shows and hip-hop tours is that he has to. This money gave him something he'd never had: a buffer. He also made a point of saying money is only part of it — the real thing is being put in the light.

44:26 Brands came back from the dead on hip-hop
Steve Stoute used business data to explain why "paying the debt" makes sense: Adidas had only 2% of the US market at the time, three-quarters of it from the Northeast, and the company just saw a bunch of people frantically buying the same shoe and throwing the laces away, with no idea why. Grand Puba's lyric "First things first, obey your thirst" later became Sprite's ad line. Tommy Hilfiger was selling ties back then and couldn't move them; driving through Harlem he saw everyone wearing their pants low with the Calvin Klein waistband showing, went back and made the underwear waistband wider and thicker and printed his own name on it, and only then did the brand take off. These brands exist because of what these people contributed.

48:31 Love isn't writing a check, it's flying to Houston
Ben told a story about his wife, who is also the foundation's chair, Felicia, to illustrate how this organization differs from other charities: Scarface had a heart problem and needed open-heart surgery, but he came from a place where people don't even really go to the doctor, he was afraid to go, and on the phone he said he wasn't going. Felicia flew to Houston and said no, you're going now. Just as they walked into the exam room, his aorta ruptured, and the doctors got him in in time and saved his life. Steve added the everyday version: she'll suddenly call to ask how you and your family are doing, and if someone in your family gets sick, flowers show up the next day, or whatever was agreed shows up.

item.title: Fashion Mogul: Stop Apologizing for Being a Working Mom, and Talk About Money
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-wsjournal-时尚大亨-当妈不必道歉-钱要开口谈/
item.description: Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money avoids them; by talking about it first, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered with, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.
item.content:encoded:
Emma Grede says if women avoid talking about money, money avoids them; by talking about it first, picking the right partners, and doing the business others can't be bothered with, she turned overlooked customers into loyal repeat buyers.

Medium information density. The first half is about brands and partnerships; the second half, on money mindset and maternal guilt, is the more valuable part. Good for a commute.

3:18 A celebrity is an accelerator, not a partner
Grede says that if you throw a star and a brand together expecting to make money or build credibility, you will quickly find it doesn't hold up. A celebrity buys you one burst of exposure and attention, but it doesn't keep customers; only a strong loyalty to a good product brings them back. That's why she insists on treating the Kardashian sisters as real business partners rather than spokespeople — the partnership has to be bigger than ‘someone's follower count’. She admits she was lucky to find partners capable of doing that.

4:19 Target a market nobody is seriously serving
Grede says that before any business she looks at the competitive landscape first, and knows what is declining and what might be needed. When Good American entered the plus-size market in 2016, the whole industry treated it as a ‘bonus 15%’ giveaway, and even today's talking points didn't exist. She believes it was rewriting the rules completely in a space where nobody was innovating and customers weren't understood that made the company work. She stresses that she never watches fashion week and never chases trends, because ‘if you're led by trends, you'll die very quickly’.

7:28 The harder the business, the more it's worth doing
On Off Season sportswear, Grede says women are badly overlooked in fan merchandise: the stands are full of women, and women control the household's purchasing decisions, yet all they can buy is generic hoodies and oversized T-shirts. She sees that as a huge business opportunity. She also admits that negotiating licenses with the NFL, NBA and WNBA is ‘not a question of spending money, it's extremely hard to do’, but what excites her is precisely doing things that require huge investment and can bring huge returns — provided you really understand where the opportunity is, and don't cut corners.

10:31 If you don't talk about money, money avoids you
Grede says that managing hundreds of employees and sitting on several company boards, she has observed a pattern at work: avoid conversations about money and money will avoid you. Men talk about money anywhere, anytime — mortgages, credit card rates, investment opportunities, big and small; women lack enough of those conversations, and enough specifics. She believes the money stories we hear growing up stay with us unless someone tells us something different. That's why she does a podcast and wrote a book: to break that silence rather than hoard the information.

13:46 What she cares about is the path to ownership
Asked about her net worth, Grede says the figure Forbes reported ‘missed a bit’, but her favorite line is ‘who cares about those valuations’. What she really cares about is the path to ownership: as a school leaver with very little education who came to America less than a decade ago, by any normal logic those numbers shouldn't belong to her. She deliberately and consciously put herself in that position, took on a lot of risk, and made a lot of trade-offs. She also pushes back on the idea that you can manifest your way to millions, saying that doesn't work.

15:48 Maternal guilt is a story handed down to us
Grede says that guilt is a story passed down through generations of grandmothers and mothers, with a default logic: if you're in New York and away from your kids, you should feel enormous guilt. But she says she actually enjoys it — three nights in a hotel, sleeping diagonally across the whole bed. She thinks many women actually feel fine about being away from their kids for a few days, it's just not cool to say so. She acknowledges she has childcare, infrastructure and a good partner, so she doesn't live in a permanent state of apology, and says she has cleared that behavior out of her thoughts and her catchphrases.

17:49 A three-hour mom at most — a joke, and also true
Grede explains her ‘three-hour mom at most’ line: she works Monday to Friday, and not nine to five, so by Saturday she isn't going to sit with her kids all day or make the whole weekend revolve around them — by noon she's ‘had enough of you lot’. She says it's a joke, but it's also saying: you're allowed to be honest about parenting differently, and a different way doesn't make you a good or bad mother. She thinks the better question is ‘what don't you do, and where do you spend your time’, which is more useful to any woman.

19:50 Women keep putting the rules on trial themselves
Asked how she differs from Lean In or Girlboss, Grede says she doesn't think she offers anything new, she just tells her own truth, and has the chance to tell it more fully than a 30-second video. She thinks the topic lingers in pop culture because we can't accept it — the rules set for women are constantly judged, discussed and argued over by women ourselves, and some of the responsibility is ours. She says every man in the room probably has no idea what she's talking about and just thinks ‘so what, carry on’. She argues for accepting that our ways differ, while the goal is shared: more women in power is a good thing.

item.title: AI labs are handing over control, and the faster the better
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-ezra-ai-实验室正把控制权交出去-而且越快越好/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-ezra-ai-实验室正把控制权交出去-而且越快越好/
item.description: Labs say AI might exterminate humanity while handing it the job of writing code, because whoever achieves recursive self-improvement first wins. This isn't an accident — it's the product roadmap.
item.content:encoded:
Labs say AI might exterminate humanity while handing it the job of writing code, because whoever achieves recursive self-improvement first wins. This isn't an accident — it's the product roadmap.

This is a monologue-style commentary with a clear position, not an interview. High information density, but only one voice in the room and no counterargument.

2:03 Slowing down isn't enough — the goal is control
