2:01 2027 is an early batch of the 2035 goals
The PLA advances on rolling three-year nodes: 2020 completed mechanization (Jerry's jab is that this means "figuring out what everyone else figured out in World War II"), then it pulled the most critical pieces out of the 2035 goals and moved them forward to form the 2027 goals, which land as three strategic capabilities: strategic counterbalance, strategic decisive victory, and strategic deterrence and control. Strategic decisive victory maps to Taiwan, strategic counterbalance maps to keeping the United States out, and nuclear is only one piece of it.

7:21 Only about 1% of Taiwanese want to join China
Responding to the Atlantic article claiming Taiwan's morale is collapsing and it will surrender to China, Jerry says nearly every analyst who has actually spent time in Taiwan and studied its government and social movements is taking it apart. The number he gives: about 1% of people today want to join China. He also points to a common mismatch — many China analysts assume they are also Taiwan analysts, but Taiwan's government system is completely different from a party-state system.

9:26 Firepower strikes have never forced a surrender
The high-intensity U.S. strikes on Iran failed to achieve their objectives, and Jerry says PLA professional journals have been tracking that kind of case. His judgment: people have said air power could end everything since the invention of the airplane, and the same goes for missiles, but in history firepower strikes have not succeeded even once — in the end you still need ground troops, you still need occupation. The role of firepower strikes is to pave the way for joint operations, not to produce political submission.

28:49 Anti-corruption isn't self-harm, it's the precondition for 2027
Against the claim that PLA corruption shows it can't fight and the purges only weaken it, Jerry says the simplest explanation is usually right: corruption is a long-standing, openly known problem, and promotions run on bribes. His example: in 2024 CMPR pointed out that 320 newly built missile silos were unusable for a period — if the silos don't work, you can't talk about strategically counterbalancing the United States. To fight joint operations, you can't be calling in fire support through connections.

37:07 China's nuclear threshold is set below 10 kilotons
China defines "low yield" as below 10 kilotons — by the comparison used on the show, Hiroshima was about 20 kilotons, so the threshold itself is still "a lot of boom", just smaller than the hundreds-of-kilotons scale of modern nuclear weapons. Paired with regional-range, higher-precision systems like the DF-26, the use of low-yield precision nuclear weapons is not to fight an all-out nuclear war but to respond to the threat of limited U.S. nuclear use, to "cover" the nuclear layer so that conventional operations can proceed.

38:08 China has never said it wants to exceed the U.S. and Russian arsenals
The common outside inference is that "China is building more nukes, so obviously it wants to surpass the United States", but the speaker says he has never seen anything close to that in Chinese nuclear literature. The original text explicitly says "we do not need that, we do not want that"; what is wanted is more and better, capabilities covering a number of "qualitative categories", used to strategically hedge against the United States. So if the United States merely builds another thousand warheads, it cannot stop China from launching missiles under warning; building another thousand ships would be more effective, because that is the lane of conventional warfare.

41:11 The Rocket Force isn't a one-shot volley, it's harassment fire throughout
The common framework is that the Rocket Force delivers one massive firepower strike and then the landing happens. But on this account the first wave is only the beginning: after it comes sustained harassment fire, plus targeted re-strikes against "something popped up and moved, and now we know where it is". So a large stock of munitions has to be held in reserve, and the Rocket Force's role runs through the entire operation, not just the opening blow. And you can't look only at the Rocket Force — it has to be placed within the broader "joint firepower strike": the PLA Ground Force has a large amount of artillery that can reach the whole island.

item.title: Treating service as a cost center is the biggest misjudgment in business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-twist-把服务当成本中心-是商业上最大的误判/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-twist-把服务当成本中心-是商业上最大的误判/
item.description: Products and brands will always be surpassed; the only long-term moat is making people feel seen — and that can be systematized like dropping a coin in a parking meter, no budget required, just care.
item.content:encoded:
Products and brands will always be surpassed; the only long-term moat is making people feel seen — and that can be systematized like dropping a coin in a parking meter, no budget required, just care.

Medium information density. The first half is a collection of hospitality cases; the second half, on fair use of AI and running a restaurant, is more worth hearing.

4:05 Product moats get filled in sooner or later
Will Guidara's judgment: no matter how good your product or how strong your brand, time proves someone will make a better product and a stronger brand — maybe with more capital, more creativity, or simply better than you. So the only competitive advantage that lasts comes from hospitality: continuously and generously investing in relationships. He concedes that anyone who achieves even a little success did it by being "unreasonable" in their investment in product and service; he is only arguing that you shouldn't save your best effort for the product alone, but also invest it in how people feel.

17:16 Hospitality can be systematized, not left to flashes of inspiration
One-off surprises like the hot dog or the first dance are hard to scale and can't be forced, or they look calculated. But Guidara says these are evidence that "you can systematize hospitality": do pattern recognition, find the moments that recur, then write "how to respond gracefully" into the process. When guests kept needing to put coins in the parking meter, the rule became: every time it happens, go put the coin in for them. Once hospitality is written into the system, the team actually gets inspired to be more hospitable — because seeing the gratitude on a guest's face after you feed the meter is a high you want to experience again and again.

24:18 No airline has ever built a business around crying babies
Guidara points to a gap he calls "criminal": flying across the US with a one-year-old is agony, yet no airline hands earplugs to the surrounding passengers, offers parents any help, or even has milk when you ask. He calls this a failure of pattern recognition — a recurring scenario everyone knows about, and nobody catches it. Jason adds: this requires budget from the top, say $250 per person per month to spend on guests, with the front line deciding how to use it; employees will love the job for it, and guests will become loyal.

34:24 When a pet dies, Chewy sends flowers to the door
Chewy's auto-subscription dog food has one inevitable moment: after the dog dies, the owner's first instinct isn't to cancel — they wait for the next bag to arrive, remember, then call to ask for a return. Chewy's response is fixed: they can't take it back, but they'll refund it and suggest donating the food; within a day or two, flowers arrive at the house. Guidara's read: this person will get another dog, and the dog food will only ever come from Chewy, with no other brand considered. That's pattern recognition, a recurring moment, and systematized kindness all holding true at once.

36:24 They stole his story, then made him a producer
The Forks episode of The Bear is basically taken from this book, rewriting the hot dog story as a deep dish pizza story. The show gave Guidara the cut long before it aired to confirm he was okay with it; he is close with those people and later became a co-producer on seasons three and four. Jason uses this to bring up AI and copyright: being technically able to do something doesn't mean you should, and legality is only the floor of morality. Guidara's landing point — they could have made him feel robbed, but chose to make him part of it.

53:31 Ending tipping requires two preconditions to hold at once
Guidara eliminated tipping at Eleven Madison Park, which he calls the most successful tipping removal ever; but after he sold the restaurant, the new owners brought tipping back, because the restaurant wasn't doing as well as before. His conclusion: eliminating tipping demands that you run the business extremely well, or it backfires. Two preconditions must be true — demand is high enough that guests don't mind a price increase; and you must stay consistently full, because you're covering tips for the team, and one slow night means you eat the loss directly. He also says they folded the service charge straight into the prix fixe price, and guests sometimes insisted on pressing cash into their hands; the team's favorite game was finding a way to slip it back into a pocket or bag before they left.

56:33 On scalping restaurant reservations, he says flatly: it's wrong
On the secondary market for reservations at places like Eleven Madison, Guidara's position is "I hated it." The reason: he priced the experience as high as possible while still offering excellent value, and if a guest pays someone else $200 before even walking in, he can no longer deliver matching revenue and value. He admits the logic is contradictory: someone else made money, you paid voluntarily, so what right does he have to stop it? He still thinks it's wrong; he adds that if he were still running a restaurant, there would be plenty of other things more worth his time and energy.

1:03:36 New York commuter rail hides a minute of grace
A recent newsletter from Guidara is about commuter rail like Metro-North and Amtrak: the system has "a minute of grace" built in — the timetable says 11:45 departure, but it always actually leaves at 11:46, to leave room for the person sprinting through the doors at the last second. He says that since learning this, he looks for his own "minutes of grace" in dealings with other companies and his own. Jason's echo is direct: not wasting time at an airport gate or on a train is the lifelong optimization of every New Yorker.

item.title: Pacing Is a PR Failure; Cyberattacks Are the Real Risk
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-a16z-ai-放慢节奏是公关失误-网络攻击才是真风险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-a16z-ai-放慢节奏是公关失误-网络攻击才是真风险/
item.description: Frontier labs packaging safety as pacing pleases no one; the real emergency is CVE weaponization compressing from years to minutes, while enterprises still have no agents, only faster search.
item.content:encoded:
Frontier labs packaging safety as pacing pleases no one; the real emergency is CVE weaponization compressing from years to minutes, while enterprises still have no agents, only faster search.

The Databricks CEO lays out pacing, the RSI test, the cyberattack curve, enterprise agent adoption and cost governance in one pass — the ontology and harness mechanics in the back half are the most valuable part.

0:00 Pacing is a PR failure, not a safety strategy
Ali argues that frontier labs packaging "safety" as "pacing" is a textbook PR failure. Pacing is orthogonal to safety — you can build weapons slowly, and that is no different from building weapons; and these companies have been running at full speed and buying more compute, so nobody believes the pacing talk. The result pleases no one: doomers don't think it's a pause, and policy people don't think you know how to do it. What they should be saying, he argues, is "secure the frontier," not "pace the frontier."

12:24 RSI only counts if four conditions hold at once
Ali gives four criteria for judging whether recursive self-improvement is happening, and all must hold simultaneously: the next generation of models requires fewer resources (GPUs) to train, takes less time to train, is smarter/more accurate, and these three things can repeat over and over. If any one fails, the system self-limits — for instance, with constant resources it hits a hardware wall. He stresses that "software writing software" is already happening, with over 90% of software at Databricks written by AI, but that is not the same as superintelligence.

15:24 The cost curve for frontier training runs the other way
Sarah points out that the compute bar for training frontier models keeps rising, from 100 million to 1 billion, and now roughly 5 to 10 billion. Ali adds: there are only one or two such training runs a year, and they violate all four criteria — they need more resources, more people, are more fragile, and require building data centers, networking and fault tolerance. Several have blown up, and failure means burning enormous sums. So the reality is "slower, more fragile, harder," not "faster, cheaper, smarter."

24:40 Weaponization time for a vulnerability went from years to hours
Ali gives this curve: in 2018 and 2019, a CVE took roughly two to three years from disclosure to weaponization; by 2022 it was down to eight or nine months; from 2022 to now it has compressed to essentially hours, almost no time at all. The reason is that data and AI are merging with the cybersecurity market — companies run large numbers of agents internally, generating massive logs and traces, and the volume of data that needs analysis is orders of magnitude larger than a year or two ago.

32:44 Say AI will destroy the world, then ask for IPO allocation
Ali concedes two things can be true at once: some people really are scared by AI risk, and some people want regulation to "pace us" — because slowing down benefits them. People can always reconcile self-interest and fear into a harmonious whole in their own heads, he says. The industry has long had this marketing play: train a new model, shout about how terrifyingly good it is, and the world's attention arrives. But he also gives the other side: the time from CVE to actual weaponized exploit went from years to minutes in three or four years, and cyberattacks are real. So "scary" is both a genuine risk and excellent marketing.

39:50 Enterprises have no agents, only faster search
Ali polled the room live: asked how many in the audience manage hundreds or thousands of agents coordinating and negotiating with each other, and almost no hands went up. Most enterprises use Microsoft Copilot, which is essentially a chatbot — "a very, very glorified efficient Google search." Coding is the only scenario that has truly landed, and even its ROI is debatable. He thinks the reason isn't that models aren't smart enough, but that models lack the organization's internal context: they haven't sat in every meeting, don't know what's in everyone's head, don't know the processes. Every organization has a few employees who know everything, and when you tap them on the shoulder you think, "what if he quits?" Pour that context into today's frontier models and you get enormous productivity — and that doesn't require a smarter model.

47:01 Ontology is that employee who's been there five years
Ali explains ontology with a concrete picture: two people equally smart, equally hardworking, with identical educational backgrounds — one on their first day, one who has been there five years. The difference is that the latter knows how the organization runs, who people are, how things get done — "don't look at the org chart, don't ask that guy, he can't get anything done." That is ontology: tacit knowledge scattered across everyone's heads. He contrasts it with the state of agents today: the agentic loop looks up resources one at a time, like Google crawling ten sites live on every search, taking ten minutes, and then handing you ten blue links — expensive, slow and bad. Google's answer was the index, and AI needs that index computed offline too, only harder — because of permission constraints, since data I can access isn't necessarily data you can access, and the object types go far beyond web pages.

56:08 Same model, different harness, nearly 2x the cost
Databricks' answer is a full cost-governance stack: Unity Gateway provides token capacity for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok and open-source models, sets budget caps and alerts by person and by group, does cost forecasting analytics, and adds intelligent routing to switch to cheaper models when nearing budget or when the question is simple. Ali gives a concrete number: the same model, the same version, changing only the harness, can differ in actual cost by nearly 2x. Their in-house harness is called Omnigent, which can multiplex across different harnesses. The result: token usage keeps rising, but AI costs are roughly flat.

item.title: AI demand still runs ahead of supply, but the compute bottleneck is turning into a political problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-mastersinbiz-ai-需求仍跑在供给前面-但算力瓶颈正在变成政治问题/
item.description: Glen Kacher of Light Street sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the first leg is done; the real risk is not over-investing in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.
item.content:encoded:
Glen Kacher of Light Street sees AI as a 15-to-20-year rebuild of the computing stack, and only a third of the first leg is done; the real risk is not over-investing in CapEx but power and local politics slowing construction.

A tech hedge fund investor in the heart of Silicon Valley strings AI compute, semiconductors, open-source models and the power bottleneck into one investable chain of judgment, at high information density.

7:16 Buy only the best company, never the second or third
Over 13 years at Integral Capital, Kacher made 46 private investments, and the lesson he drew is: do not buy the second- or third-best company in an industry, always buy the best one you can get. The reason is that in tech the leader takes two-thirds of the market, the number two gets 20% to 25% at most, and everyone else fights over scraps. Higher margins plus a dominant share compound the lead. But he also concedes that incumbents in tech get disrupted, and disruption usually comes not from big companies but from small ones — AI and the semiconductors behind AI are the test case for that rule.

8:17 Nvidia's moat is underappreciated
Kacher says many people assume Nvidia will lose its roughly 85% share of the AI accelerator market, and the shift to inference does give competitors an opening. But he thinks the market currently underappreciates Nvidia's own capacity to innovate. He describes the evolution of inference chips as an alphabet progression from CPU to FPU to GPU to XPU, where X stands for the unknown: Google has TPU, there is Trainium and various other approaches, and Nvidia itself acquired the Grok inference line. He judges that inference will ultimately be a bigger market than training, so there will be many chip forms and many opportunities to innovate.

21:51 Four semiconductor companies are 40% of the portfolio
TSMC, Nvidia, Broadcom and AMD make up about 40% of Light Street's public holdings, a highly concentrated portfolio. Kacher's logic: concentrate capital where innovation is densest, and right now the densest place is the core of AI accelerated computing. Nvidia has more than 80% of the GPU networking market, and AMD is catching up; as agentic AI becomes the next leg of growth, AMD has a unique advantage because it is one of the two big players in both desktop and server CPUs; Broadcom has built TPUs for Google for years and now has opportunities with big players like OpenAI; TSMC fabs for all three, so it wins no matter who wins, an almost oligopolistic or even monopolistic position.

26:01 Open-source models are fighting a price war
Kacher thinks the battle between Anthropic and OpenAI is happening in real time, and Google remains a player thanks to Gemini and its search distribution advantage, so it cannot be ruled out. But the battlefield that is really emerging is open-source models: they are free, can be downloaded to run on local hardware, or run on someone else's commoditized hardware in the cloud, competing directly with the two big companies' expensive frontier models. He judges that early signals show both approaches have their place. At the same time he points to the regulatory problem: open-source models can be put inside your own software and tuned to your needs, and regulators actually have few options, because these models are already out in the wild.

33:14 Someone was saying GPUs should do AI back in 2005
Kacher recalls that at Integral, Kleiner Perkins partner Bill Joy mentioned a group of engineers at Caltech using GPUs for early AI computation, around 2005 or 2006, and Bill Joy's conclusion was that GPUs would be the chip architecture best suited to AI computation. It stayed in his head. Later, on every visit to Nvidia, Jensen would talk about AI, but at the time AI was only a tiny end market for Nvidia, and crypto mattered far more. In the second half of 2022 the crypto crash and the takeoff of AI happened at the same time, and the market was more focused on crypto and pushed the stock down, which gave them the chance to build a position in Nvidia.

45:36 The giants are not over-investing, they are catching up
Faced with the challenge that AI could be over-provisioned like fiber, Kacher's answer is: Amazon, Microsoft and Google are building the compute stack in partnership with Anthropic and OpenAI, and the question is how far ahead of demand they plan. His judgment is that today they are not ahead, they are behind and catching up. The bears expect them to over-invest, but that is not happening today. He concedes there are real bottlenecks, including the memory companies and TSMC, which cannot invest as fast as they would like, so today demand still runs far ahead of supply, and the pessimism around AI is misplaced.

52:47 A fifteen-year cycle, and only a third is done
Kacher likens AI to the shift from client-server to internet architecture, a computing cycle that happens roughly every 15 to 25 years. The old technology was a search-and-retrieve model, with data stored in databases; AI generates a custom answer to your question and your data on every use, and is far more compute-intensive. The rhythm he gives: infrastructure development takes about 5 to 10 years, years 6 to 16 are when the platform or operating system takes shape, and years 11 to 21 are when applications become the main venue for enterprise investment and innovation. By that framework, roughly a third of the first leg is done, and the whole cycle is at least 15 to 20 years.

53:48 Power and local politics have become the new bottleneck
Kacher treats political resistance to data centers as a real risk: any bottleneck that slows technology adoption is a problem. He says it is not yet a big problem today, but it is an emerging one. His solution is that the industry has to explain itself proactively: Northern Virginia, as the data center capital of the world, has brought the area tax revenue and blue-collar demand for electricians, plumbers and construction workers, a shot in the arm for the economy. He mentions a data center project in San Mateo that plans to put Bloom Energy natural gas fuel cells behind the meter, with almost no emissions and almost no noise, and residents still opposed it because they had "heard data centers are bad." He sees this as an education problem, requiring project-by-project explanation of energy, jobs and tax revenue, from local to national.

item.title: The Pizza Tracker: How We Were Trained to Pay for Fake Progress Bars
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-planetmoney-披萨追踪器-我们被驯化成愿意为假进度条买单/
item.description: Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.
item.content:encoded:
Domino's pizza tracker started as an internal management tool and became a global app standard. It works because it turns waiting into visible work; and once companies discovered we love watching progress bars, they started faking them.

Medium information density, but the second half about "deliberate slowdowns" and "fake progress bars" is worth the price. Suited to listeners interested in product design and consumer psychology.

2:07 The 30-minute guarantee sold control, not speed
Domino's once promised delivery in 30 minutes or it was free. The guarantee made drivers speed, led to deaths and lawsuits, and was eventually dropped. But David Halbenstricker has a theory: the guarantee was popular not just because it was fast, but because it gave customers a sense of control. In the early 2000s Domino's commissioned a study and found that the customer's psychology after ordering a pizza is a roller coaster: the peak is at the moment of ordering, then it slides all the way down — "Where's my pizza? Did they lose my order?" No matter how long the actual wait, what customers hate is the process of waiting.

8:16 The internal tool had to work first, before the customer side
Executives at the time did not want to build a pizza tracker, because tracking every pizza at every store was too time-consuming and looked like a gimmick. What they were really obsessed with was "out-the-door time." A UK franchisee put the out-the-door times of five to ten nearby stores on a single display so they would compete with each other, and gave cash rewards to the top-ranked stores. After David's boss visited the UK, he had David replicate the system in the US. David connected every store's out-the-door time to a central system and turned it into a real-time dashboard. The CEO said it was the thing that drove performance most during his tenure.

11:25 The tracker was a byproduct of the internal system
David and a colleague realised they already had a system tracking every pizza, so they decided to "hitch a ride" and build a customer-facing tracker. In 2006 most people didn't have smartphones; FedEx, UPS and Amazon could track packages, but on a timescale of days, not minutes. Real-time tracking of pizza progress was entirely new. The designer's interface looked like a horizontal thermometer: from order, prep, bake, box to delivery, each completed step turned the next segment red. When David saw the mockup he said: "That's a hot dog. We're a pizza company, why is there a hot dog?" But executives liked it, and decided to launch before the Super Bowl.

15:36 Designers use the pizza tracker as a meeting prop
Shuya Gong was a design director at IDEO and later taught design at Harvard. Consulting for many companies in the mid-2010s, she found one of the most effective ways to open a meeting was to order a pizza on the spot, project the tracker onto a big screen, and ask the client: "How do you feel right now?" She says you can feel the anxiety rise or fall very viscerally in your body, feel the reassurance and groundedness. Then you can ask: which of those parts do you want your users to feel when they use your product? The pizza tracker became shorthand in her design circle: whenever a client involved waiting, she'd say "they need a pizza tracker."

17:39 The tracker manufactures a "labor illusion"
Shuya says one reason the pizza tracker is popular is that as shopping experiences become more digital, the tracker replicates something important from the physical world — watching other people work. Online experiences lack that visibility, so people get impatient more easily. Researchers found that reminding customers there is labor behind a product makes them value it more; they call it the "labor illusion." Shuya also describes a more mysterious mechanism: the tracker changes our perception of time. Like walking somewhere, the return trip feels shorter because it's familiar and has landmarks. The pizza tracker gives us a familiar route and landmarks — pizza being made, on the road, being delivered — making the wait feel shorter.

19:47 Banks deliberately slow transfers to fake a wait
Working with banks and fintech companies in the mid-2010s, Shuya found their problem was the opposite of Domino's: customers weren't used to transfers being too fast. Two computers talk, confirm the amount, and the money is there — no road to cross, no cheese to melt. But for people used to money taking a while to arrive, instant arrival "feels suspicious." So companies deliberately slow down the "money tracker," giving you no real-time feedback but adding a buffer that makes you wait. Shuya says this is intentionally slowing down time, adding meaningful friction so that in the waiting you feel the seriousness and weight of the transfer. The host pressed: isn't this advising lying to customers? Shuya said she prefers to understand it as "curating the experience," adding back the physicality that existed in the traditional experience, to make people comfortable.

21:48 TurboTax and Uber progress bars may be fake
TurboTax pops up an animation during tax filing saying "We're checking your deductions and credits." But a few years ago someone looked at the code and found the animation is identical for everyone, in every situation, and takes the same amount of time. The question is: is TurboTax trying to reassure us during the terrifying process of filing taxes, or using the labor illusion to make us feel that paying a big bill is worth it? Uber is similar: the host repeatedly received updated pickup times, but the car almost always arrived later than promised. It felt like the tracker was part of a deliberate deception — to make you choose Uber over Lyft, to keep you from cancelling, to get you standing on the street early. The show reached out to TurboTax and Uber; TurboTax did not respond, Uber did not arrange an interview but shared some data suggesting their pickup times are fairly accurate.

25:52 Field test: the pizza tracker is mostly real
Nick biked to a local Domino's to stake it out, while Alex ordered a half-Hawaiian, half-pepperoni pizza at home and monitored the tracker in real time. Nick ordered a pepperoni pizza in the store as cover. The tracker showed "Ivan" making the pizza, but when Nick asked the staff their name, they said "Alex." The tracker also showed a "quality check," but Nick saw no quality inspector. David had explained, though, that because Domino's uses conveyor ovens, the bake time is nearly fixed, so the tracker automatically jumps to the next step after a set time. Eventually the pizza came out, was boxed, and was driven off by Alex (aka Ivan), with Nick chasing on his bike and nearly being taken for a stalker. Alex pressed "delivered" at Nick's door and the tracker updated quickly. Conclusion: the tracker is mostly accurate, but "Ivan is making it" and "quality check" are fake.

item.title: AI Proves in Half an Hour a Math Theorem Humans Couldn't Crack in a Year
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-instituteforad-ai-半小时证出人类一年没做出的数学定理/
item.description: A stuck L^p problem: AI delivers a five-page proof in half an hour, compresses a 60-page paper down to its core lemma, and casually pushes the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.
item.content:encoded:
A stuck L^p problem: AI delivers a five-page proof in half an hour, compresses a 60-page paper down to its core lemma, and casually pushes the threshold for continuous density from 588 to 9.

If you care about what AI can actually do in pure mathematics, this episode gives a concrete, verifiable case: not assisted computation, but a proof structure a human didn't think of.

0:18 For the first time, AI had a good idea
The speaker says this is the first time he has encountered a model that "really had a good idea" on a problem he had worked on for a long time, and that the idea led to "very elegant efficient progress." Note his wording: it isn't that AI did the computation for him, it's that AI produced a proof approach he hadn't thought of. He credits the result to Astra, and says it was done only last week.

8:13 The key theorem: absolute continuity automatically carries L^p
The core theorem is: if a self-similar measure μ is absolutely continuous, then its density automatically lies in some L^p with p greater than 1. What actually excites the speaker isn't the fact itself but that p is quantitative — p can be expressed explicitly in terms of the mass μ gives to small balls. Because p is quantitative, one can bring over the methods used to study explicit absolute continuity, construct explicit L^p examples, and from there get to continuous density.

12:27 p can never be made uniform
The speaker specifically warns: p can never be made uniform. For any dimension d and any p greater than 1, there exists some self-similar measure that lies in L^1 but not in L^p. So this quantitative result must not be read as "all absolutely continuous self-similar measures have uniform L^p integrability" — it is a case-by-case bound that depends on the mass distribution.

23:45 Split λ into odd and even parts
The trick for proving continuous density: split the random series of the Bernoulli convolution into odd and even terms; after factoring a λ out of the odd part, what remains is exactly the even part. So μ_λ equals the convolution of μ_{λ²} with itself. If λ² falls in the range where Solomyak proved L^2 holds almost surely, then the convolution of two L^2 functions is continuous, and μ_λ has continuous density. This is the bridge from an L^2 result to continuity.

34:17 A 60-page paper compressed into 5 pages
The speaker says the core idea was in fact already his and his collaborator's, but that AI was "extremely elegant and efficient" in using it. Varju's paper is 60 pages, his own is also very long; AI compressed the passage from one result to another into 5 pages, and after "maybe a bit of a weakening," another 5 pages suffice to get a stronger conclusion. He stresses this is not AI thinking up the core idea for him, it's AI combining known tools in a way he "could have never" done.

36:18 Half an hour to run, 50 hours to formalise
Asked about runtime, the speaker says "not long, maybe half an hour." The whole result was then formalised in Lean, which took about 50 hours. He also mentions tricks like a goal command that let the model "really try hard." The comparison: it might have taken him a year, and "if you sent me this paper to referee, I would like who is this person?"

39:21 The continuous-density threshold moves from 588 to 9
For the case λ = 1 - 1/n, AI proves μ_λ is continuous when n is greater than 588 — the speaker says this is not yet the result of him pushing the constant, "if I push the constant, I could easily push the constant more." Even more striking is another result: absolutely continuous when n is greater than 9, which the speaker says "I could not dare think I could prove"; he himself pushed for two and a half hours to get to 9, while the ideal target is 3.

43:23 The key lemma comes from an obscure paper
The heart of the proof is a lemma from geometric measure theory: for an L^1 positive function f, if the mass of a set inside a small ball is small and the integral of f over that set is also small, then f lies in some explicit L^p, with p given explicitly by C, ε, A. The speaker says the lemma is "not too difficult to prove," about a page, but "extremely difficult to find because it's not a very well-known fact" — it was dug out of some random papers.

item.content:encoded:
Chuck Jones said the key to animation isn't what a character looks like or how it's drawn, but "who he is" — he understood the character first, which is how Daffy could be cowardly and overbearing at once, and how Bugs Bunny had to be provoked before he fought back.

The first half, the Chuck Jones interview, is dense with information; the second half, the Cassandra Wilson segment, is mostly music appreciation, so you can listen to just the interview portion.

0:00 Bugs Bunny's violence wouldn't pass review today
Comedian Dustin Nickerson tried showing classic cartoons to his young daughter and found they hadn't become harmless with time: plenty of characters have speech impediments, and the behavior is highly aggressive. Pepe Le Pew physically holds a female character so she can't leave, while other characters murder each other — the Coyote wants to kill the bird. This runs counter to the cartoon impression in viewers' memories that "everyone is friends."

4:04 A shelved Warner film was saved by an independent distributor
After Coyote vs. Acme was finished, Warner Bros. Discovery shelved it and wrote it off for financial purposes. This year an independent distributor bought the rights for $50 million, and last month it finally opened. The film played in relatively few theaters across the US, but it has already recouped almost its entire cost domestically, with another $30 million overseas. The movie itself is about the Coyote suing the Acme Corporation, inspired by Ian Frazier's 1990 parody piece in The New Yorker.

7:07 Daffy is cowardly and overbearing at the same time
Chuck Jones said what makes Daffy funny is that he rushes in and fears to take a step at the same time, is sycophantic and domineering at the same time — like when we go into the boss's office to ask for a raise, domineering at the door and sycophantic once inside, except with Daffy both happen at once. He admitted he couldn't understand "crazy" characters, so he always had to "pasteurize" a character and figure out who he is. He stressed that the point of character animation isn't what the character looks like, nor how it's drawn, but "who he is."

9:11 Bugs Bunny is a comedy hero, not a comedy loser
Jones first did Duck Amuck with Daffy, then later did Rabbit Rampage with Bugs Bunny, and the same setup didn't hold, because Bugs isn't that kind of character. He classed Bugs as a comedy hero, whereas the line of comedians running through Chaplin and Buster Keaton are half-losers, more like the rest of us. He liked Daffy because Daffy keeps going forward, to the point where Jones himself would stop for fear of what others would think.

10:14 A two-hour "yes session" where no one may say anything negative
After 1946, Warner's cartoons were directed by three men: Fritz Freeling, Bob McKimpson and Jones. Whoever had an idea for a film called the other directors and the writers into a meeting they called a "yes session": for two hours no one was allowed to say anything negative, and if you had nothing to contribute you shut up. The result was that everyone worked on everyone else's films, but each director had absolute control over the content of his own, and there was no infighting among them. Jones also admitted that if a good gag he'd given was used by Freeling and the audience laughed, he naturally wanted to go throw up — that's human nature, and it was the Daffy in him.

13:25 The narrower the rules, the better the comedy
Jones believed that in comedy, the more you narrow and restrict a character, the better it works: once Chaplin put on the Little Tramp outfit, what he could do was locked down. Once Roadrunner and Coyote were fixed in the American Southwest desert, the rules followed — Roadrunner has to stay on the road, can never harm Coyote, and Coyote can only harm himself by buying those unlucky Acme products, with no sound in the whole film but "beep-beep." Bugs Bunny is too strong and easily becomes a bully, so every film first lets him live his own life in his natural rabbit environment until someone comes to take his hide or his life, and only then does he fight back.

16:30 Hiding one dirty frame in a twenty-fourth of a second
Jones admitted that Warner's animators all drew that kind of pornographic cartoon on the sly. He himself would sometimes slip a single frame — a twenty-fourth of a second — of something dirty into a Pepe Le Pew film, then call the office manager over and say there seemed to be a little glitch here that he couldn't figure out. He knew no one could see it, but the manager would be shocked on the spot. He always kept a replacement frame on hand just in case, but he enjoyed doing it, in his words, to "reduce him to moccasins."

17:31 The networks cut films until they were incomprehensible
Jones said his scenes and lines were never censored; that was left to the "brilliant people" at the networks, and what they cut made the whole film incomprehensible. Both CBS and ABC did it. What he found absurd was that the Roadrunner series, the most complained-about for violence, actually has no violence — Roadrunner never harms Coyote, and Coyote is simply the victim of his own incompetence.

item.content:encoded:
In 2025, fewer than 1% of IMO contestants scored full marks on Problem 6, and every AI got stuck on it. What makes it hard is not computation — it is that you must first understand, first have taste, and only then put pen to paper. And that is exactly what reinforcement learning has the hardest time training.

The bulk of this episode is a complete walkthrough of one math problem, not AI industry analysis. Only the last 5 minutes discuss the relationship between AI and math, but those 5 minutes are worth hearing.

0:00 What blocks AI is not computation, it is patience
On 2025 IMO Problem 6, of more than 600 top contestants worldwide, fewer than 1% scored full marks. By 2025, models from several institutions could already answer every other problem correctly, and got stuck only on this one. DeepMind research director Thang Luong's explanation: the model has no patience — it will not spend time understanding the problem or developing a feel for it, but starts solving immediately. Karpathy adds a second reason: the model has no sense of "what makes a problem or a strategy beautiful," and the solution to this problem depends precisely on aesthetic judgment.

6:11 Genius is really the residue of experience
Facing this problem, the most obvious construction is to put all the X's on the diagonal and cover the remaining region with horizontal tiles, giving 2(n-1) pieces. But this construction is too obvious to be the answer IMO wants. Karpathy inserts a seemingly unrelated cube-cutting brain teaser here: a 3x3x3 cube cut into 27 small cubes, where you may rearrange the pieces after each cut — what is the minimum number of cuts? The answer is 6, because each of the 6 faces of the very center small cube needs its own separate cut. This proof idea — fix your attention on one face of the internal structure — is exactly the key to the tiling problem that follows.

12:17 The most efficient tiling has every tile touching four X's
Highlight all four edges of every X, and each time you place a tile, switch off the edges it touches. In an inefficient tiling, a tile touches only 1 or even 0 X's; in an efficient tiling, every tile touches 4 X's. This yields a conjecture: the optimal tiling should make as many tiles as possible touch 4 distinct X's. But look further: an X cannot fall in the middle of a tile's edge — that would make the two tiles above and below conflict on the left, since a single column cannot contain two X's. The X must fall on a corner of the tiles, with four tiles pinwheeling around it. Using square tiles of side length k, you can tile a large grid of side length k². And 2025 happens to be 45², a coincidence that makes the construction look extremely promising.

19:27 Highlight only one direction and the proof misses the tiles on one side
Highlight the edges of all X's, 4k² in total, each tile touches at most 4, subtract the 4 on the boundary that need not be touched, and you get the lower bound k²-1. But the target lower bound is k²+2k-3, off by a term proportional to k. The problem is that only the right edges are highlighted: the correspondence you get this way is tight on the right side of the diagram, but misses a large number of tiles concentrated on the left. Switching to any other single direction is the same — the missed tiles always cluster on one side. Karpathy says mathematics rewards you for respecting symmetry and punishes you for not respecting it — pick an arbitrary direction, and the weakness shows up in the inequality.

27:38 Cut the grid into four regions, highlight each edge only once
The solution is to draw two paths: one going up-right along the X's, one going down-right, dividing the whole diagram into four regions. If an X is in the right region, highlight its right edge; if in the top region, highlight its top edge; left, right, top and bottom each govern one region. An X lying on a boundary highlights two edges. This both supplies the missing highlighted edges and guarantees that each tile touches at most one highlighted edge — because when a tile sits in the left region, the X above it cannot highlight its bottom edge, the X below it cannot highlight its top edge, and the X to its left cannot highlight its right edge. This diagram is the core of the entire proof.

31:48 The problem reduces to a pure permutation problem
Label each X with the number of the row it sits in; since each row contains exactly one X, these labels form a permutation of 1 to k². The up-right path corresponds to an increasing subsequence, the down-right path to a decreasing subsequence. Let LIS be the length of the longest increasing subsequence and LDS the length of the longest decreasing subsequence; the total number of highlighted edges is then k² + LIS + LDS - 4 (plus 1 more when the two paths intersect, making it -3). To prove the target lower bound k²+2k-3, it suffices to prove LIS + LDS ≥ 2k, that is, that the average of the two is at least k. At this point the grid has completely disappeared, and what remains is a pure fact about permutations.

39:59 The proof of Erdős-Szekeres is itself a gem
This pure permutation fact is the Erdős-Szekeres theorem: in any permutation, the product of the lengths of the longest increasing subsequence and the longest decreasing subsequence is at least the length n of the permutation. An IMO contestant can simply cite the theorem and finish, but Karpathy chooses to give the proof as well. The method is to label each position with a pair of numbers: the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending there, and the length of the longest decreasing subsequence ending there. Because the numbers in a permutation are all distinct, the two label pairs at any two positions must differ — if the later number is larger, the first label increases by at least one; if smaller, the second label increases by at least one. Plot these label pairs as coordinate points: the longest increasing subsequence is the width of the bounding box, the longest decreasing subsequence is the height, and width times height equals the number of lattice points, which is the length of the permutation.

48:08 Beyond the proof there is another layer: making the proof feel obvious
Karpathy says knowing a proof is only a very small part of deeply understanding mathematics. When he and Nishad Dulkhar made this video, their first reaction on seeing the original proof was "I know it's true, but how would anyone come up with this." What they wanted to contribute was not a new proof but a narrative, so that when viewers arrive at the proof it no longer feels like it came out of nowhere. He has a name for this: motivated explanation. This bears directly on AI and mathematics: if a machine can generate proofs but does not bring human understanding, then it has completely lost its meaning. And academia has long used "proof" as a proxy metric for progress, which exposes an urgent need — for a new, independent way to measure whether a publication actually advances human understanding.
